item.title: Downtown, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Downtown, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $710,647, up 0.56 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Downtown Oakland's commercial centre was fixed at Ninth Street and Broadway by 1877, and Broadway has been the spine ever since.

The district grew along the 7th Street railroad line in the 1870s, and the oldest surviving piece of it is the six blocks now called Old Oakland, between Broadway, Jefferson, 7th and 10th, where the Victorians from the 1870s and 1880s are still standing. The Nicholl Block dates to 1878. As the city expanded northward the old core was left behind, went economically depressed, and sat with vacant buildings for decades, and that neglect is the reason the nineteenth century architecture survived at all. Restoration of 9th Street between Washington and Broadway in the 1970s and 1980s produced the block called Victorian Row.

What downtown is now is the densest part of Oakland: office buildings, two BART stations, civic buildings, and residential towers and converted lofts among the older stock.

Almost nothing here is a single family house. Oakland has 191,713 housing units and only 41.5 percent are single family detached, with owner occupancy at 42.3 percent citywide, and downtown sits far below both. 46.6 percent of the city's housing predates 1950.

So this is a condominium and loft purchase, and the building matters more than the unit.

Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the monthly dues, because the reserve position is what becomes a special assessment. Ask what the association insures and what you insure. Ask whether the building has had a seismic retrofit and whether it is classified soft story or unreinforced masonry, since downtown has a lot of both and the answer affects financing, insurance and your own exposure.

Ask what is entitled on the parcels around you. Downtown is where Oakland approves height, and a view is not a protected asset.

Oakland's transfer tax runs 16.10 dollars per thousand at the citywide typical value, and the bracket applies to the whole price, so check your number against the next threshold before you set it.

Then stand on the street at nine on a weeknight. Downtown empties, and you should know what that version feels like.

What the market is doing right now

Downtown sits at $710,647 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.56 percent since last month and up 0.6 percent since last year.

Listing activity in Oakland for 2026-09. Active inventory is 527. 316 new listings came on, and 228 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $674,250 at $494 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $710,647, up 0.56 percent month over month, up 0.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,190, or $86,280 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.71 percent (Oakland effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Oakland I cover, and what each one is:

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Downtown home and the monthly carry lands near $7,190. That is $86,280 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $11,441 in transfer tax on a $710,647 sale here, at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $5,721 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $2,000,000 the rate steps from 16.10 to 18.60 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $2,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $10,660.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $9,161, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $27,880.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/oakland/downtown/.

item.title: Old Oakland, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Old Oakland, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $710,647, up 0.56 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
This is where Oakland actually started, and the Victorians are still standing because the city moved on and left them alone.

Old Oakland is six blocks bounded by Broadway, Jefferson, 7th and 10th Streets. The commercial district grew along the 7th Street railroad line in the 1870s, and by 1877 the hub was established at Ninth Street and Broadway. Most of the buildings you see went up in the 1870s and 1880s, among them the Nicholl Block from 1878.

Then the city grew uptown and this district stopped being the centre. It became economically depressed and a lot of the buildings sat vacant for decades. That neglect is exactly why they survived. Nobody had the money or the reason to tear them down and put up something taller. In the 1970s and 1980s developers restored the block of 9th Street between Washington and Broadway, and it has been called Victorian Row since.

So what exists here is a concentrated run of nineteenth century commercial architecture in a downtown. That is rare in California, because most cities replaced theirs.

The residential inventory is almost all lofts and condominiums converted out of or built among those commercial buildings. Oakland has 191,713 housing units with 46.6 percent predating 1950, and in this district the share is near total.

What to do about that. On a converted loft or a condominium in an older building, the first question is the building, not the unit. Get the association budget and the reserve study. Ask what the association insures and what falls to you. Ask directly whether the building has had a seismic retrofit and whether it is classified soft story, because unreinforced masonry and soft story construction both affect financing, insurance and your own risk, and a nineteenth century commercial building is a candidate for both.

Ask about the mechanical systems too. Conversions put residential plumbing, electrical and HVAC into shells never designed for it, and the quality varies enormously.

Then walk 9th Street between Washington and Broadway on a Friday evening. That block is the argument for living here.

  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.

item.title: Chinatown, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Chinatown, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $334,594, down 0.66 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Oakland Chinatown is older than almost everything around it. By 1860 there were about 200 Chinese residents in a city of roughly 1,500 people.

The community settled around 8th and Webster Streets and built a business centre there that is still the centre today. The neighborhood is one of the oldest continuously occupied Chinatowns in the country and it never became primarily a tourist district. That is the usual fate. It is a working commercial neighborhood with grocers, herbalists, restaurants and family associations.

The twentieth century cost it a great deal of ground. The Laney College and Chinatown redevelopment plan and the construction of BART in the early 1970s cut through the neighborhood. One local history puts the displacement at around 10,000 residents, and the losses included the Ming Quong Home, an orphanage for girls at 51 Ninth Street. Redevelopment of that era is the single biggest reason the street pattern here is interrupted the way it is.

The housing is dense and old. Oakland has 191,713 housing units with 46.6 percent built before 1950, and in Chinatown the stock skews older and overwhelmingly multi unit. Owner occupancy citywide is 42.3 percent and in this part of the city it runs far lower.

So this is an income property and condominium market more than a single family one, and the rules are the first thing to learn.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city on any building, and read Oakland's rent adjustment program and just cause for eviction rules before you model income, because they apply to most of this stock and they are not optional. Ask whether the building is unreinforced masonry or soft story, since both are common in pre 1950 commercial and mixed use buildings here and both affect financing and insurance.

Get the permit history, and on a mixed use building ask the city what the ground floor is legally permitted to be.

Then spend a Saturday morning at the 8th and Webster markets. The commercial density is the asset here and it does not read in photographs.

What the market is doing right now

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.

  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.

item.title: Jack London, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Jack London, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $710,647, up 0.56 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Jack London drank in a bar down here that is still open, and he put it in his books seventeen times.

Johnny Heinold opened the First and Last Chance Saloon on this waterfront in 1883, though one city history gives the date as June 1, 1884. London was a local kid and the saloon became his base. It is the setting behind scenes in The Call of the Wild and The Sea Wolf, it gets referenced seventeen times in John Barleycorn, and it has been nicknamed Jack London's Rendezvous ever since. The floor still slopes from the 1906 earthquake.

Everything else about this district follows from the water. It was working port and warehouse ground, and the Amtrak station is here. That makes it the one Oakland neighborhood where you can walk from your door to a long distance train.

The housing is almost entirely converted warehouses and newer construction: lofts, condominiums and apartment buildings put into or built beside industrial shells. That is unusual for Oakland, where 46.6 percent of the 191,713 housing units predate 1950 and most of the older stock is houses instead of warehouses.

So shop it as a loft and condominium market with industrial neighbours, and ask the industrial questions.

Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask what the association insures. Ask whether the building has had a seismic retrofit and whether it is soft story or unreinforced masonry, because converted industrial buildings are frequently both and it changes your financing.

Ask the city what the surrounding parcels permit, because this is a working port district and the use next door can change in ways a residential neighborhood's cannot. Then ask about noise and about freight and train movement at the specific address, at night.

And on anything near the estuary, get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire.

Then go sit in Heinold's for twenty minutes. The building is a listed piece of Oakland and it costs you the price of one drink to understand the neighborhood's whole history.

item.title: Lake Merritt, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Lake Merritt, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $674,272, up 0.68 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
In 1870 the California legislature made this lake the first wildlife refuge in North America. Nothing else in the country had that protection yet.

Samuel Merritt had proposed it the year before. One account puts the official designation at March 18, 1870. Worth knowing: the 1870 law did not actually use the words wildlife refuge, so the protection started out looser than the anniversary plaques suggest. What is not in dispute is that the lake sits on the Pacific Flyway, the main north and south route for birds along the west coast, and that is why the protection mattered and still does.

The other thing on the shore is stranger and more consequential. Children's Fairyland opened here in 1950, a storybook theme park conceived by a local business owner named Arthur Navlet. Walt Disney came to look at it while he was working out his own park, and Disneyland opened five years later. The small park on the north shore of a lake in Oakland is part of the ancestry of the whole modern theme park.

The neighborhood around the lake is the densest residential ground in Oakland: apartment buildings and condominiums of every era, from 1920s courtyard buildings to recent towers, wrapped around a tidal lagoon with a three mile path on it.

Oakland has 191,713 housing units and 46.6 percent of them predate 1950. The newer cities in this county are the reverse of that. Around Lake Merritt that share runs higher still.

So the questions here are the multi unit and pre war questions. On a condominium, get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues number, ask what the association insures and what you must, and ask directly about any seismic retrofit history, because lenders ask about soft story construction on older buildings and the answer affects your financing.

On a small apartment building, confirm the legal unit count with the city and read Oakland's rent adjustment and just cause rules before you model a single dollar of income. They apply to most older buildings here and they are specific.

Then walk the full loop around the lake once. It is three miles and it is the reason people pay to be here.

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.

  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.

Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.

item.content:encoded:
In the early 1950s Frank Sinatra had trouble with his voice, and he flew a woman from Oakland out to Las Vegas to fix it. Her studio was a small dim room on College Avenue. Judy Davis taught out of that room for about fifty years, and the people who came through it include Barbra Streisand, Judy Garland, Grace Slick and Eddie Money. She got into the work the hard way: a tonsillectomy at nineteen damaged her own vocal cords and left her with a rasp, so she went and studied anatomy and built a method out of it. She was still teaching two weeks before she died in 2001, at 81.

College Avenue has always kept things like that in plain sight. Walk up it and you pass a Julia Morgan building at 5951. The congregation hired her in January 1917 on a ten thousand dollar budget, and she gave them a church with no steeple. She repeated triangles through the structure instead, and set a round window over the entrance. Morgan is the Hearst Castle architect and the first woman licensed to practice architecture in California. This is one of her quiet ones, and most people drive past it.

Half a mile west, where Broadway crosses Pleasant Valley, there is a shopping center sitting in a hole. The Bilger quarry worked that site on and off from 1870 to 1946 and was for years the largest rock quarry in Alameda County. Drive on an older street in North or West Oakland and you are driving on crushed rock that came out of that pit. The pond at the east end never drained. The Claremont Country Club owns it and uses it to irrigate the golf course.

The name is older than the quarry and it is completely literal. Rockridge sits on a shutter ridge thrown up by the Hayward Fault. The west side of the fault creeps north every time it moves, and the ridge has been shoved far enough across Temescal Creek to dam it, so the creek turns and runs north to get around the obstruction. Geologists call it a shutter ridge because it slides across the valley like the shutter on an old box camera. That is why the streets bend the way they do up here. It is also worth knowing before you waive an inspection.

Then there are the stairs. Developers cut hundreds of public staircases into these hills so people living up the slope could get down to the streetcars on the main road, and Upper Rockridge ended up with more of them than almost anywhere in the city. The Key System ran up College Avenue. Once everyone had a car the stairs stopped mattering and sat forgotten for decades. Oakland counts about 220 of them and rebuilt roughly 40 between 2001 and 2017. Several are still unmarked dirt and still officially public right of way, so you can walk them today if you know where they start.

The houses came in behind the streetcar. Rockridge Park was the first residential tract in 1909, and the bungalows and Craftsman cottages on the flats near College went up through the 1920s, with white stucco Spanish Colonial Revival mixed in among them. Highway 24 was cut straight through the neighborhood in the 1950s. The Claremont branch library has been open on College since 1924. St. Albert's Priory, a Dominican monastery, has been on Birch Court since 1931. Market Hall opened in 1987 and is a covered row of separate stalls, not one grocer. BART opened at 5660 College in 1973, and that station is why a lot of people here pay what they pay.

Here is what you are actually buying. Pre-war construction, a commercial street you can do on foot without doubling back, and a train that runs under the Bay in one direction and out through the Caldecott to Orinda and Walnut Creek in the other. You are also buying a short list of items that turn up on nearly every original house on these blocks. Knob and tube wiring where nobody rewired. Galvanized supply lines. Original foundations with no seismic bolting, an insurance problem as much as a structural one. Clay sewer laterals, certified at sale under Oakland's ordinance and a routine line item, not a surprise. Single pane original windows, usually the feature a buyer most wants to keep and the one that most moves the heating bill.

Go walk an untouched Craftsman and a renovated one in the same week. The gap between those two numbers is the entire negotiation, and reading the inspection report is how you win it.

What the market is doing right now

Rockridge sits at $1,802,087 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.66 percent since last month and up 10.3 percent since last year.

Listing activity in ZIP 94618 for 2026-09. Active inventory is 21, up 90.9 percent from the prior month and down 40.8 percent from a year earlier. 18 new listings came on, up 12.5 percent month over month, and 5 went pending. Median days on market is 19, up 18.8 percent month over month and down 15.6 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,179,250 at $634 per square foot, on a median listing of 1,889 square feet. Typical rent in the same area is $2,987, up 3.9 percent year over year.

  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.

The man who designed Central Park designed the cemetery at the top of this street.

Mountain View Cemetery was founded in 1863 and the commission went to Frederick Law Olmsted. It covers somewhere between 220 and 226 acres depending on the source, and it was dedicated in 1865, with the first burial that same year. Accounts differ on the exact day. The ridge section, where the crypts get grand and the view runs west across the bay to the San Francisco skyline, has been called Millionaires' Row for a century. There is also an unmarked piece of ground called Stranger's Plot holding about 200 unknown burials.

The names in it are the names in this whole project. Julia Morgan is buried there, the first woman licensed to practise architecture in California, who designed Hearst Castle and also the 1917 church at 5951 College Avenue in Rockridge. So is Charles Crocker of the Big Four, the syndicate that bought Alfred Cohen's railroad in 1868 and let him build the Fernside mansion in Alameda. So is Samuel Merritt, the Oakland mayor who proposed protecting the lake that carries his name. And Domingo Ghirardelli.

Piedmont Avenue itself is the commercial street running south from the cemetery gates, annexed by Oakland in 1897 along with Temescal, Golden Gate and Bushrod. It is a walkable strip of small storefronts set at the sidewalk.

The housing is pre war and mixed: houses on the side streets, apartment buildings and small income properties closer to the avenue. Oakland has 191,713 housing units and 46.6 percent of them predate 1950.

Charles Alexander Klinkner founded the place in 1885 on about 150 acres and put his own name on it. By 1888 the residents had renamed it Golden Gate, possibly after the Golden Gate Hotel on San Pablo Avenue. The old families simply preferred it to Klinkner's.

Only 41.5 percent of units are single family detached and owner occupancy is 42.3 percent citywide.

So the legal unit count comes first on any address. The 16th Street Station opened in 1912 as the western terminus of the transcontinental line, a Beaux-Arts building by the architect Jarvis Hunt and once the largest Southern Pacific station in Northern California. It also became the western headquarters of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, the union the porters organised in 1925 and the first Black union in the country. Its headquarters were in Chicago, but its vice president was based in Oakland. C. L. Dellums worked as a Pullman porter from 1924 to 1927 and was let go partly for openly supporting the union. He was elected a vice president in 1929 and later became its president, in 1968 by one account and 1966 by another. He was the uncle of Ron Dellums, later a congressman and mayor of Oakland.

The station took damage in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake and closed soon after. Amtrak had already moved its trains to Jack London Square and Emeryville during the 1980s. The building is on the National Register and it is still standing, still empty, and still the subject of a restoration campaign.

Prescott runs from Mandela Parkway east to Frontage Road west, between West Grand Avenue and 7th Street, and it takes its name from the Prescott School. Seventh Street was the music district. In the 1940s and 1950s it was lined with jazz clubs and bars and people called it the Harlem of the West.

item.title: McClymonds, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the McClymonds, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $567,543, up 0.49 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Bill Russell went to high school here. So did Paul Silas, Joe Ellis, Antonio Davis, Wendell Hayes and Marcus Peters.

McClymonds started in January 1915 in a small building at 12th and Market that Oakland Technical High School had just moved out of, with sixty students. It opened as a vocational school and it was the first public school in California to offer summer school. The name honours John W. McClymonds, who ran the Oakland schools as superintendent from 1889 to 1913 and pushed for the school's creation. The campus moved to 26th and Myrtle in 1924. In its first thirty six years the school changed location five times and operated under eight different names. In 2005 it was split into two small schools, BEST and EXCEL, under Oakland's Small Schools Initiative, and the campus has since been through a three phase modernisation covering building systems and code compliance.

A school that produced that list of athletes is the landmark of this neighborhood, and the neighborhood carries its name.

The housing around it is West Oakland stock: Victorian and early twentieth century, dense, much of it divided into flats. Oakland has 191,713 housing units, 71,234 of them built in 1939 or earlier and 18,124 more in the 1940s, so 46.6 percent of the city predates 1950. Only 41.5 percent of units citywide are single family detached and owner occupancy is 42.3 percent. Both figures run lower here.

So the first questions are regulatory, not cosmetic.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing. Get the permit history. Ask whether the building is nonconforming, since that limits rebuilding after a loss and affects both financing and insurance. If it holds more than one unit, read Oakland's rent adjustment program and the just cause for eviction rules before you model income.

Then the pre war list, and it is long on stock this old: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the sewer lateral Oakland certifies at sale, and the condition of original siding and windows.

Oakland's transfer tax runs 16.10 dollars per thousand and the bracket applies to the whole price. Check your number against the next threshold.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical McClymonds home at $567,543 on 2026-09-30, up 0.49 percent month over month and down 6.9 percent year over year.

Listing activity in Oakland for 2026-09. Active inventory is 527. 316 new listings came on, and 228 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $674,250 at $494 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $567,543, up 0.49 percent month over month, down 6.9 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $5,911, or $70,929 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.71 percent (Oakland effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Oakland I cover, and what each one is:

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $5,911, $70,929 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 16.10 dollars per thousand, a $567,543 sale in McClymonds carries about $9,137 in transfer tax. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $4,569 each, though the contract decides.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $2,000,000 the rate steps from 16.10 to 18.60 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $2,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $8,513.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$88,253 here. The five year figure is -$240,203.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

Dogtown is a nickname, and the official name of this ground is Clawson.

The boundaries given for Dogtown run from Adeline Street on the east to Mandela Parkway on the west, and Mandela Parkway is where the Cypress Street Viaduct used to stand. As for where the name came from, the common story is that Oakland police coined it over a population of stray dogs in the early 1980s, and the source that carries that story flags it as needing a citation. The verifiable history here is the freeway. The Cypress structure ran through West Oakland from the 1950s, split the neighborhood, and collapsed in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. item.content:encoded:
Hugh Dimond came over for the Gold Rush, made money in the Mariposa and Tuolumne mines, and in 1867 bought 267 acres of Oakland foothill along Sausal Creek.

The district carries his name and so, for a while, did the creek. Locals called it Dimond Creek well into the period when maps said Sausal. The city bought the land that is now Dimond Park in 1917, about a dozen acres of it depending on which source you read.

The creek is the reason the neighborhood is shaped the way it is. Sausal Creek runs out of Dimond Canyon, and that canyon was the main route the redwoods came down. The first steam sawmill in the area went up in 1850 at Palo Seco Creek, at the head of the canyon, and a logging road ran from there to a wharf at the foot of 13th Avenue. The San Antonio redwood forest that covered these hills was gone inside about fifteen years.

The commercial heart is the intersection of Fruitvale Avenue and MacArthur Boulevard. As far back as 1940 that corner was described as the entrance to the Dimond District, and it still works that way. The district sits about two miles east of Lake Merritt, north of Fruitvale and west of Laurel.

item.title: Redwood Heights, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Redwood Heights, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,041,330, up 0.75 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Ships entering San Francisco Bay used to steer by two redwood trees standing on this ridge. The trees were that big.

Blossom Rock sat submerged west of Yerba Buena Island and it wrecked hulls. Navigators learned to line up on a pair of giant redwoods in the Oakland hills to clear it, and the state record says those trees were in use as landmarks until at least 1851. Then the loggers got them. One account puts the cutting after 1851 and before 1854, and the state record says the original stems were gone by 1855. What stands at the site today are sprouts from the original stumps, and the spot is a California Historical Landmark in Redwood Regional Park. Blossom Rock itself was dealt with in 1870, when US military engineers under Robert S. Williamson blew enough of it away to stop it being a hazard.

That is the history of this whole ridge in one object. The San Antonio redwood forest covered these hills from Shepherd Canyon southeast, logging started around 1847, the first steam sawmill went up in 1850 at the head of Dimond Canyon, and the forest was level inside about fifteen years. The neighborhood is named for trees that were cut down before it existed.

The housing is twentieth century, built on the logged ground, on streets that bend with the grade. Oakland has 191,713 housing units and 46.6 percent predate 1950. Up here the stock skews later than the flats and is more consistently single family.

So shop it as a hill purchase. Ask for the soils and drainage history on the parcel, because on sloped ground the dirt is the expensive part. Ask about any retaining structures, who owns them and what condition they are in. Ask where water goes in a wet month.

Get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire and ask the broker to explain the risk rating, because this is hill ground against regional parkland.

Then drive up to the landmark and look at the sprouts. The original trees were navigation aids for ocean shipping, and they stood where your street is.

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.

  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.

The San Francisco and Alameda Railroad built the station here in 1865 and named it Jones. Four years later it became Elmhurst. The town around it was farmland, and it stayed its own place until Oakland's largest annexation swallowed it. item.title: Toler Heights, Oakland: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Toler Heights, Oakland housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $594,329, up 0.96 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Toler Heights is the far southeastern corner of Oakland, on rising ground above the flats, and its published history is thin, so this is the development record and the practical read.

The name describes the ground. This is hillside at the city's edge, up against San Leandro, and the grade is what distinguishes it from the Deep East Oakland flats below. Oakland reached this far south through its 1909 annexation, the largest the city ever undertook. It brought in Elmhurst, Fruitvale, Melrose and Fitchburg, carried the city from 22.9 square miles to roughly 60, and followed a population that doubled to 150,174 by 1910 as people resettled after the 1906 earthquake.

The housing is predominantly postwar single family on sloped lots. Oakland has 191,713 housing units, 71,234 of them built in 1939 or earlier and 18,124 in the 1940s, so 46.6 percent of the city predates 1950. Up here the stock runs later than that, 41.5 percent of city units are single family detached and the share is higher on this kind of ground, and owner occupancy citywide is 42.3 percent and also runs higher on the hill.

So shop it as a hillside purchase, because that is what sets the cost.

Ask for the soils and drainage history on the specific parcel. Ask who owns and maintains any retaining structures and what condition they are in, because a failing retaining wall is the single most expensive surprise on a hill lot and it is frequently a shared obligation. Ask the inspector where water leaves the property in a wet month.

Get a written insurance quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire, and ask the broker to explain the risk rating, since hill ground at the city's edge is priced differently from the flats.

Then the house itself, on postwar stock: the roof, the supply lines, the electrical panel capacity, the furnace and the water heater, plus whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

Then drive the route in and out once after dark and once in the rain. On hill streets at the edge of a city, that trip tells you something a daytime showing will not.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Toler Heights home at $594,329 on 2026-09-30, up 0.96 percent month over month and up 0.4 percent year over year.

Listing activity in Oakland for 2026-09. Active inventory is 527. 316 new listings came on, and 228 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $674,250 at $494 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $594,329, up 0.96 percent month over month, up 0.4 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $6,150, or $73,802 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.71 percent (Oakland effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Oakland I cover, and what each one is:

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $6,150 a month, $73,802 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. Alameda County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $594,329 here, transfer tax runs about $9,569 at 16.10 dollars per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $4,784 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $2,000,000 the rate steps from 16.10 to 18.60 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $2,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near $5,557. At five years it reaches $16,875.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

There is a sealed railway tunnel 3,700 feet long running under these hills, and its west portal is near the corner of Saroni Drive and Shepherd Canyon Road.

The Oakland and Antioch Railway dug the Redwood Peak Tunnel between 1910 and 1913 to carry trains under the Oakland hills toward Contra Costa County. The line that used it became part of the Sacramento Northern, and it ran right through Montclair Village and up Shepherd Canyon, crossing into Montclair on a trestle near Moraga Avenue and Thornhill Drive where a pocket park now marks the spot. Sources disagree on when service started, with 1911, 1912 and about 1913 all given, and passenger service ended in either 1940 or 1941. The last train went through in 1957 and the tunnel was sealed.

You can walk the right of way. The Montclair Railroad Trail runs from behind the Village up Shepherd Canyon with interpretive panels along it.

Montclair Village itself is the commercial centre of the Oakland hills, a genuine walkable district of small storefronts in a part of the city that is otherwise all car.

Then there is 1991. On the morning of Sunday, October 20, 1991 a grass fire that had been knocked down the day before near the Caldecott Tunnel came back to life shortly before eleven. Winds gusting to 65 miles an hour drove it down the south ridge of Claremont Canyon, and inside thirty minutes it had jumped Highway 24 and Highway 13 and set hundreds of houses alight. By the time it was fully controlled on October 23 it had killed 25 people, injured 150, and destroyed 2,843 single family homes and 437 apartment and condominium units. Losses ran to about 1.5 billion dollars. Cal Fire lists it as the Tunnel Fire and the cause was never determined. Montclair was among the neighborhoods where hundreds of houses burned, so the stock here is a mix of pre fire survivors and post 1991 rebuilds, sometimes on the same street.

  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.

  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.

item.content:encoded:
Sequoyah looks down on the old naval hospital site from the ridge above Interstate 580.

The hospital below is the defining neighbour. A country club occupied that ground until the Great Depression closed it, the Navy built Oak Knoll Naval Hospital on the 167 acre site in 1942 to treat personnel wounded in the Pacific, and it ran until 1996 when the 1993 base closure round shut it. That site is now under redevelopment. It is the single biggest variable in this neighborhood for the next decade.

Grass Valley sits alongside, and the Oakland Zoo is in it.

The neighborhood itself is hillside residential on the southeastern edge of Oakland, above the freeway, with the regional parkland of the ridge behind it.

Oakland has 191,713 housing units and 46.6 percent of them predate 1950, but up here the stock runs later and is predominantly single family on sloped lots. Owner occupancy citywide is 42.3 percent and runs considerably higher on this kind of ground.

So three things before you buy, in this order.

Read what is entitled on the Oak Knoll site and on the parcels around your address. The documents are public, the project has been through years of process, and what gets built there changes your traffic and your outlook.

Get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire, with the risk rating explained and the defensible space requirements confirmed. This is hill ground against open space on the Oakland ridge and the 1991 firestorm reshaped how carriers price the entire east side of this city.

Then the hillside list: soils and drainage history for the parcel, the condition and ownership of any retaining structures, and where water leaves the property in a wet month.

Then drive your commute down to the freeway at your real hour. On this ridge the on ramp is the whole calculation.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Sequoyah home is worth $994,344. That is up 0.40 percent on the month and up 0.6 percent on the year.

Median asking price is $674,250 at $494 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $994,344, up 0.40 percent month over month, up 0.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $9,726, or $116,715 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.71 percent (Oakland effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Oakland I cover, and what each one is:

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Caballo Hills. Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $9,726 monthly, or $116,715 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Alameda County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $16,009 in transfer tax on a $994,344 sale here, at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $8,004 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. Woodminster takes its name from the amphitheatre in Joaquin Miller Park on the ridge above it, and the published history on the neighborhood itself is thin, so this is the development record and the practical read.

The San Antonio redwood forest covered this ground until loggers levelled it inside about fifteen years from the late 1840s, with the first steam sawmill going up in 1850 at the head of Dimond Canyon and a logging road running down to a wharf at the foot of 13th Avenue. The parkland on the ridge today is second growth on that cut ground.

Then the fire. On the morning of Sunday, October 20, 1991 a grass fire that had been knocked down the day before near the Caldecott Tunnel came back to life shortly before eleven. Winds gusting to 65 miles an hour drove it down the south ridge of Claremont Canyon, and inside thirty minutes it had jumped Highway 24 and Highway 13 and set hundreds of houses alight. By the time it was fully controlled on October 23 it had killed 25 people, injured 150, and destroyed 2,843 single family homes and 437 apartment and condominium units. Losses ran to about 1.5 billion dollars. Cal Fire lists it as the Tunnel Fire and the cause was never determined. item.content:encoded:
Caballo Hills is a hillside pocket at the southeastern edge of Oakland with very little published history, so this is the development record and the buying read.

The ground is the story. These ridges carried the San Antonio redwood forest until it was logged out inside about fifteen years from the late 1840s. What stands now is second growth and mixed woodland, with regional parkland along the ridge and the city dropping away below.

The 1991 firestorm is the governing modern fact for everything on this side of Oakland. On the morning of Sunday, October 20, 1991 a grass fire that had been knocked down the day before near the Caldecott Tunnel came back to life shortly before eleven. Winds gusting to 65 miles an hour drove it down the south ridge of Claremont Canyon, and inside thirty minutes it had jumped Highway 24 and Highway 13 and set hundreds of houses alight. By the time it was fully controlled on October 23 it had killed 25 people, injured 150, and destroyed 2,843 single family homes and 437 apartment and condominium units. Losses ran to about 1.5 billion dollars. Cal Fire lists it as the Tunnel Fire and the cause was never determined. Even where a specific street was untouched, that event set how carriers price this entire ridge.

The housing is later single family on sloped lots, planned in layout, and a good deal of it sits inside homeowner associations. Oakland has 191,713 housing units and 46.6 percent predate 1950, but up here the stock is newer than the city average. Owner occupancy citywide is 42.3 percent and runs higher on this kind of ground.

So four things, in this order, before the house itself.

Fire insurance: a written quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire, with the risk rating explained, the defensible space requirement confirmed, and a straight answer on which carriers write this zone.

Homeowner association: get the budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask specifically what the association is responsible for on the slopes, because on hill ground that can include drainage and retaining structures.

Hillside: soils and drainage history for the parcel, the condition and ownership of any retaining structures, and where water leaves the property in a wet month.

Then the house, matched to its year built, and a drive in and out at your real commute hour after dark.

  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.71 percent (Oakland effective rate).

  • Acorn. Fifty blocks of this neighborhood were demolished.
  • Adams Point. Adams Point is named for Edson Adams, one of the men who got hold of Oakland's land early, and in 1906 it filled up with San Franciscans who had nowhere else to go.
  • Allendale. The Allendale tract map was recorded in 1892, and there was a cinema operating here by 1913.
  • Brookfield Village. Twelve hundred houses went up here during the Second World War and they sold for four thousand dollars each.
  • Bushrod. Bushrod was annexed by Oakland in 1897, in the same batch as Temescal, Golden Gate and Piedmont Avenue, and that date is the most solid thing in its published record.
  • Castlemont. Castlemont takes its name from the high school at its centre, and its published history is thin enough that this is the development record and the buying read.
  • Chabot Park. Anthony Chabot dammed a creek in 1868 and built Oakland its first water supply at municipal scale, and his name is on the parkland at the edge of this neighborhood.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly $5,172 in price and payment combined, and five years to $15,663.

Shattuck Avenue is wide and straight through downtown because it was a railroad before it was a street.

The Berkeley Branch line was completed in 1876, and its alignment is what became Stanford Avenue, Adeline Street and Shattuck Avenue. Stanford Avenue carries the name of the railroad's president, Leland Stanford. Shattuck reads as a corridor instead of an ordinary city street because it was laid out to carry trains into the center of town, and the commercial district grew along it.

The rail history kept layering. Electric streetcars reached this part of the East Bay in 1891. The Key System ran its own tracks down Shattuck parallel to the Southern Pacific line. Streetcar service across the system ended in 1948, replaced by buses. Then BART put a station under Shattuck downtown, and the corridor has been a transit spine continuously for about a hundred and fifty years under four different technologies.

What downtown is now is the densest part of Berkeley: the BART station, the commercial core, civic buildings, and the university campus immediately east.

The housing is almost entirely multi unit, and a good deal of it is newer construction, because downtown is where Berkeley has concentrated the housing it has added.

So this is a different purchase from anywhere else in the city, and the questions change accordingly. On a condominium, get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not just the monthly dues, because the reserve position is what produces a special assessment later. Ask what the association insures and what you have to insure. Find out whether the building has any seismic retrofit history, since older multi unit buildings in California carry that question and lenders ask it too.   • Gilman District. Green Day's original graffiti is on a beam above the stage at 924 Gilman Street, from back when they were called Sweet Children.

item.content:encoded:
North Berkeley's housing stock has a hard line running through it, and the line is a single day in 1923.

On September 17 that year, a fire out of Wildcat Canyon crossed the ridge on a northeast wind and destroyed between 543 and 640 structures in this part of the city, about 585 of them houses. Roughly 4,000 people were put out of their homes and no one died. The water mains in the burn area were two inches in diameter. The hydrants were close to useless. The fire ran through La Loma Park and the Northside before the wind shifted and it stopped. The practical legacy is that a lot of the houses here date to the rebuild instead of to the original build.

Below the burn line, the neighborhood is the early twentieth century Berkeley that everyone pictures: brown shingle and Craftsman houses on a grid, large street trees, and a commercial cluster at Shattuck and Vine that people have called the Gourmet Ghetto for decades.

Where the land starts to climb, the rock parks begin. Mason-McDuffie donated the parcels around five volcanic outcrops to the city while developing this side of Berkeley, and they were dedicated as parks in 1917. Indian Rock and Mortar Rock are the two most people know, and the Ohlone bedrock mortars ground into Mortar Rock are still visible.

Two different buying problems, then, depending on which half you are in. On the flats, the questions are the pre war ones: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the permit history on any addition. Up the hill, add fire insurance quoted in writing on the exact address, plus soils and drainage documentation on the parcel.

Either way, pull the year built first. In North Berkeley that single number tells you which side of 1923 you are on, and it changes the entire inspection conversation.

What the market is doing right now

Berkeley voters came 194 votes short of turning this entire neighborhood into a public park, and because they missed, you can buy a house here.

item.description: What the Berkeley Hills, Berkeley housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,709,669, up 0.78 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
On September 17, 1923, a fire came over the ridge out of Wildcat Canyon and burned a large part of this area to the ground in a single afternoon.

Somewhere between 543 and 640 structures went, depending on which count you use, including roughly 585 houses. About 4,000 people lost their homes. Remarkably, nobody was killed. The fire started in undeveloped grass and chaparral, a strong northeast wind pushed it over the Berkeley Hills, and it moved through the La Loma Park and Northside neighborhoods lifting burning shakes off one roof and dropping them on the next. The water mains in the affected area were two inches across and could not feed the hydrants. It stopped when the wind changed. For sixty eight years it was the worst fire the East Bay had seen, until the 1991 Oakland hills fire took that distinction.

That one day is the most important thing to know about the housing stock up here. A large share of it was built or rebuilt in the years immediately after, so the era of the architecture on a given street is often a direct record of where the fire stopped.

The rest of what defines the Berkeley Hills is grade and view. Streets switchback, lots are cut into slope, and the houses look west across the bay.

If you are buying here, three costs sit outside the purchase price and you should price all three before contingencies are gone. Fire insurance, quoted in writing on the specific address, with the risk rating explained to you. Soils and drainage, documented for the parcel, because on a hill the ground is the expensive part. And seismic work, starting with whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

Then do the part most buyers skip. Drive your own route down the hill at the hour you would actually leave, and drive it again after dark. Narrow switchbacks are charming on a Sunday afternoon showing and they are a different proposition on a Tuesday in February.

The oldest building in Elmwood's shopping district went up in 1907, one year after the San Francisco earthquake, and that timing explains how the neighborhood filled in.

Before that, this was large rural estates. The 1906 earthquake and fire sent people across the bay in numbers, the housing boom that followed broke those estates into tracts, and Elmwood filled in. The commercial corner at Ashby and College Avenues dates from the same moment. The oldest building there, on the corner itself, was built in 1907 in Colonial Revival style with shops on the ground floor and apartments above, and that pattern is still what the block does.

The commercial strip is deliberately small. It runs along College Avenue about one to two blocks in either direction from Ashby and then stops. There is no strip center and no parking field. Everything is set at the sidewalk.

The housing came in as a streetcar suburb and it reads that way: early twentieth century, substantial, on a grid of mature street trees, most of it built inside a twenty year window after 1906. That consistency is useful, because it means comparable sales here are genuinely comparable.

What you are buying is one of the shortest walks to a real commercial corner anywhere in the East Bay, attached to a house that is probably a hundred years old or more.

So price the house as what it is. Get a specialist inspection on anything pre 1920 and ask directly about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring and galvanized supply lines. Ask for the permit history, since houses of this era in this neighborhood have usually been added onto at least once and not all of that work was permitted. Find out whether the property carries any local historic designation before you plan an exterior change.

item.content:encoded:
The Claremont Hotel could not legally serve a drink for decades, and the reason was a state law measured with a ruler.

California Penal Code section 172 banned liquor sales within a fixed distance of the University of California. The original rule reached two miles. In 1876 it was cut to one mile from the perimeter of the campus, and the hotel sat inside that circle. The law was not a Berkeley ordinance and the hotel's position on the Berkeley and Oakland line made no difference to it. In 1937 the statute was amended so the distance could be measured by road instead of in a straight line, and the hotel could finally pour. There is a well known story that a Cal student re measured the route, proved it was over a mile and was given free drinks for life. Public media that has covered it calls that a legend and at least one newspaper has run a debunking of it, so enjoy the story and do not repeat it as fact.

The hotel genuinely does straddle the city line, and the boundary follows the old Key System E train right of way across the property. That matters more than it sounds. City transfer tax is set by the city, not the ZIP code. Oakland charges 16.10 dollars per thousand at this price level and Berkeley charges 26.10. On the typical ZIP 94705 home at 1,974,361 dollars that is 31,787 dollars on the Oakland side and 51,531 on the Berkeley side, a difference of 19,744 dollars for the same house at the same price. Berkeley's rates are also scheduled to change on January 1, 2027 under Measure W, passed in November 2024, so confirm the current figure before you model anything.

The neighborhood around it is one of the most expensive in Berkeley: large early twentieth century houses, mature trees, curving streets on rising ground below the hotel.

So the single most valuable thing you can do here is establish which city your parcel is actually in before you model anything. Get it from the assessor's parcel record, not from the mailing address, because the mailing address can be Berkeley while the parcel sits in Oakland. Then run the transfer tax both ways so you know what you are dealing with. Adeline Street runs at an angle to everything around it, and the reason is a railroad built in 1876.

The Berkeley Branch line went in that year, and its route is now Stanford Avenue, Adeline Street and Shattuck Avenue. Stanford Avenue is named for the railroad's president, Leland Stanford. Adeline's odd diagonal through South Berkeley is the old right of way, still visible in the street grid a century and a half later.

The stops made the neighborhoods. Lorin sat at Adeline and Alcatraz, and until after 1900 it was a flag stop where you climbed twelve wooden steps from street level to reach the tracks. A second stop, Newbury Station, stood on Adeline just south of Ashby. Electric streetcars arrived in 1891 when the Oakland Consolidated Street Railroad laid two lines through here. In 1909 the Key System added the Ashby Avenue line, run with a streetcar so small that people called it the Dinky. The Key System's F Line used the Adeline corridor on its own tracks alongside the Southern Pacific. Streetcars stopped running in 1948 and buses took over. Santa Fe kept hauling freight along Adeline until 1979, when the operation was rerouted and the tracks came out.

Then BART. The plan was to run the line through here above ground. A campaign led by the resident Mabel Howard and the then city councilmember Ron Dellums, with Urban Care and the NAACP, got the Ashby station put underground instead. Homes and businesses next to the station were demolished for the construction.

So this is a neighborhood whose shape was set by rails four separate times, and the housing stock is accordingly mixed in both era and type.

Pull the year built and the permit history on any address here, because the range is wide and so is the construction quality. On pre war stock, run the standard list: foundation bolting, wiring, supply lines. Ask whether a building with more than one unit is legal and permitted as such.   • Berkeley Marina. There is a pier here that used to run three and a half miles out into the bay.
  • Claremont. The Claremont Hotel could not legally serve a drink for decades, and the reason was a state law measured with a ruler.
  • Cragmont. Cragmont is named for the rock, and the rock is why the neighborhood looks the way it does.
  • Downtown Berkeley. Shattuck Avenue is wide and straight through downtown because it was a railroad before it was a street.
  • Elmwood. The oldest building in Elmwood's shopping district went up in 1907, one year after the San Francisco earthquake, and that timing explains how the neighborhood filled in.
  • Gilman District. Green Day's original graffiti is on a beam above the stage at 924 Gilman Street, from back when they were called Sweet Children.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $13,384 a month, $160,606 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

item.description: What the Le Conte, Berkeley housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,442,475, up 0.90 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
The neighborhood is still called Le Conte. The school at the center of it is not.

LeConte Elementary stood at 2241 Russell Street under that name for generations. Joseph LeConte was a respected member of the UC Berkeley faculty, and he was also a slave owner and a committed supporter of the Confederacy. An effort to change the school's name got going around 2012, when the district was moving the school toward a two way Spanish and English immersion program, and in May 2018 the Berkeley school board voted unanimously to rename it for Sylvia Mendez. The Mendez family's court case ended legal segregation in California schools in 1947. Separately, in November 2020, UC Berkeley took the LeConte name off one of its own buildings along with Barrows Hall.

That sequence is a useful thing to know here, because the neighborhood name and the school name no longer match, and a buyer searching one will not always find the other.

The neighborhood itself is South Berkeley flatland between the campus area and Ashby, on a regular grid. The housing is early twentieth century for the most part, modest in scale, on small lots, with a significant share of it in small multi unit buildings and converted flats.

So unit count is the first question on any purchase here. Confirm with the city how many legal units a building has, because the number on a listing and the number the city recognizes are not always the same in this part of Berkeley. If it is more than one unit, read Berkeley's rent stabilization rules before you model income, since they are specific and they apply.

Then the age questions. Pull the year built and the permit history, and on anything pre war ask directly about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring and galvanized supply lines.

West Berkeley was a separate town called Ocean View, and it is older than the university.

Berkeley's first school, Ocean View School, opened in 1856 at Virginia Street and San Pablo Avenue. When Berkeley incorporated in 1878 the settlement was folded in and renamed West Berkeley, and it spent the next century as the industrial and working part of the city.

That industrial zoning is why West Berkeley is what it is today. Two things grew in the shell of it. The Fourth Street shopping district turned warehouse frontage into one of the better retail streets in the East Bay. And 924 Gilman Street, the volunteer run all ages punk club that opened on December 31, 1986 and launched Operation Ivy, Rancid and Green Day. Green Day's graffiti from their Sweet Children days is still on a beam over the stage.

So this is the part of Berkeley where a Victorian cottage, a steel fabrication shop, an art studio and a retail block can all sit within two hundred feet of each other.

So zoning is the first question on any purchase here, ahead of the house itself. Pull the zoning for the parcel and for everything adjacent, and ask the city what is permitted instead of looking at what is currently operating. Then the age questions: year built, permit history, foundation, wiring and supply lines, since a lot of this stock is pre 1900 and has been modified without paperwork. The stagecoach stop was William Bowen's, at today's San Pablo Avenue and Delaware Street, and Bowen's Inn opened in 1854. Delaware Street existed to connect the two. The name came from the view: on a clear day you could see the Pacific through the Golden Gate. The first school in what is now Berkeley was the Ocean View School, established in 1856 at the southeast corner of Virginia Street and San Pablo Avenue.

Dates vary across sources. The 1853 wharf is the best supported, one account puts the landing at 1854, and a library history gives 1868 for the settlement. The sequence is not in doubt even if the year is.

When Berkeley incorporated in 1878, Ocean View came in with it and the name changed to West Berkeley. From then on it was the industrial and working side of town, and that is still legible in the building stock. There is a Delaware Street Historic District here.

So the housing is Berkeley's oldest, mixed in among industrial and commercial buildings, on flat ground near the bay.

Four things to establish on any address. The year built, because some of this is genuinely nineteenth century and the inspection list is long. The permit history, since houses this old in a working district have usually been altered repeatedly. The zoning on the parcel and on the parcels around it, because mixed use means a neighbor's permitted use may not match the current one. And the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote, this being flat land close to the water.

Then walk Delaware Street. Standing where the wharf road met the stagecoach road is the shortest history lesson in the city.

  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

  • Bateman. Nobody is entirely sure who Bateman was, and the neighborhood is named after him anyway.
  • Berkeley Hills. On September 17, 1923, a fire came over the ridge out of Wildcat Canyon and burned a large part of this area to the ground in a single afternoon.
  • Berkeley Marina. There is a pier here that used to run three and a half miles out into the bay.
  • Claremont. The Claremont Hotel could not legally serve a drink for decades, and the reason was a state law measured with a ruler.
  • Cragmont. Cragmont is named for the rock, and the rock is why the neighborhood looks the way it does.
  • Downtown Berkeley. Shattuck Avenue is wide and straight through downtown because it was a railroad before it was a street.
  • Elmwood. The oldest building in Elmwood's shopping district went up in 1907, one year after the San Francisco earthquake, and that timing explains how the neighborhood filled in.
  • Gilman District. Green Day's original graffiti is on a beam above the stage at 924 Gilman Street, from back when they were called Sweet Children.

The same developer built the expensive hill subdivisions and this tract of small houses on the flats, and in both cases he put a park at the middle of it as the selling point.

The Frances Albrier Community Center was added to the park and dedicated on October 18, 1964, fifty years after the playground opened.

So the housing here is early twentieth century, modest in scale, on small flat lots on a tight grid, all of it oriented around a park at the center.

There is a pier here that used to run three and a half miles out into the bay. You can see where it goes and you cannot walk it.

Only the first three thousand feet were maintained, and even that stretch closed to the public in July 2015 once the structure was no longer sound. Filling the bay to create the marina shortened the structure to about two and a half miles.

Because the marina is built on fill well beyond the original shoreline, most of what you stand on out here did not exist a century ago. Part of the ground was the city's municipal landfill. In the 1990s that section was turned into parkland as North Waterfront Park, and it was renamed Cesar Chavez Park in 1996 for the labor leader.

So this is the edge of the city: marina, open shoreline, parkland on a capped landfill, and the stub of a ferry pier.

Very little of it is housing, and that is the first thing to understand if you are searching here. Residential inventory in this immediate area is limited and most of what people mean by buying near the Berkeley Marina is actually the flats inland of it.

If something genuinely at the waterfront does come up, three questions come before the house. Get the flood zone determination and a written insurance quote on the specific parcel, since this is made ground at sea level. Ask directly about fill and settlement history and have the inspector look at the foundation and the flatwork with that in mind. item.content:encoded:
Solano Avenue is the reason people move to Albany, and it does not stop at the city line.

Albany is a small city wedged between Berkeley and the Contra Costa line, and almost half of its housing is older than the Second World War. Solano Avenue is the commercial spine and it runs straight through into Berkeley. That is the practical fact about living here: the shopping street does not stop at the city line. Albany Hill rises at the western end, and the Albany waterfront and the Bulb sit beyond it on the bay.

Albany has 8,070 housing units and 48.7 percent of them predate 1950, one of the highest pre war shares in this series. 50.3 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 53.1 percent, the ACS median value is 1,202,200 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,445. Nearly half the stock being pre war is the single most important thing to know before you make an offer.

So run the pre war list properly. Foundation bolting first. Then knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the permit history on every addition, and the condition of original windows and siding.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, because conversions are common in stock this age and the permits often are not.

Then the lot. Check the dimensions and setbacks early if an accessory dwelling unit is part of your plan, because Albany lots are small and the setback decides it.

Then walk Solano Avenue from the front door and time it. That walk, and the fact that it carries on into Berkeley without a break, is what the Albany premium actually buys.

What to test before you pay the Solano premium. Walk the avenue from the front door of the specific address and do a real errand: groceries, a coffee, a haircut. Then keep walking east past the city line and see how far the usable stretch actually runs, because the commercial street continues into Berkeley and the useful part is longer than the Albany portion alone. Then come back at nine on a weeknight. A shopping street is a different neighbour after dark, and on a block this close to one you should know which version you are buying.

What the market is doing right now

$1,237,577 is the typical Solano Avenue district home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.59 percent, and over the year up 6.2 percent.
