  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Albany I cover, and what each one is:

  • Albany Hill. Albany Hill is the rise at the western end of the city, and it is the one piece of Albany that is not flat.
  • San Pablo Avenue Corridor. San Pablo Avenue is Albany's other commercial street and it is a very different animal from Solano.
  • The Circle. The Circle is the roundabout where Marin Avenue meets the hill, and the neighborhood around it takes the name.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $11,602 a month to own the typical home in Solano Avenue district, $139,219 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $19,925 in transfer tax on a $1,237,577 sale here, at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Convention puts about $9,962 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $18,564.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $183,865. Stretch it to five and the figure is $609,356.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

San Pablo Avenue is Albany's other commercial street and it is a very different animal from Solano.

Albany is a small city wedged between Berkeley and the Contra Costa line, and almost half of its housing is older than the Second World War. Solano Avenue is the commercial spine and it runs straight through into Berkeley. That is the practical fact about living here: the shopping street does not stop at the city line. Albany Hill rises at the western end, and the Albany waterfront and the Bulb sit beyond it on the bay.

Albany has 8,070 housing units and 48.7 percent of them predate 1950, one of the highest pre war shares in this series. 50.3 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 53.1 percent, the ACS median value is 1,202,200 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,445. Nearly half the stock being pre war is the single most important thing to know before you make an offer.

So run the pre war list properly. Foundation bolting first. Then knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the permit history on every addition, and the condition of original windows and siding.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, because conversions are common in stock this age and the permits often are not.

Then the lot. Check the dimensions and setbacks early if an accessory dwelling unit is part of your plan, because Albany lots are small and the setback decides it.

Then walk Solano Avenue from the front door and time it. That walk, and the fact that it carries on into Berkeley without a break, is what the Albany premium actually buys.

San Pablo Avenue is the other kind of commercial street: wider, faster, more mixed in use, and carrying through traffic instead of foot traffic. That changes two things for a buyer. Pull the zoning for the parcel and for everything touching it, and ask the city what is permitted next door instead of reading what operates there now, because a corridor like this carries uses a residential block does not. And go stand at the address in the evening and listen, because proximity to an arterial is the single most common thing buyers underestimate and the easiest to check.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in San Pablo Avenue corridor is $1,237,577 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.59 percent from the month before and up 6.2 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Albany for 2026-09. Active inventory is 25. 18 new listings came on, and 9 went pending. Median days on market is 25.

Median asking price is $669,000 at $602 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,237,577, up 0.59 percent month over month, up 6.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $11,602, or $139,219 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Albany I cover, and what each one is:

  • Albany Hill. Albany Hill is the rise at the western end of the city, and it is the one piece of Albany that is not flat.
  • Solano Avenue District. Solano Avenue is the reason people move to Albany, and it does not stop at the city line.
  • The Circle. The Circle is the roundabout where Marin Avenue meets the hill, and the neighborhood around it takes the name.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $11,602 monthly, or $139,219 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. In Alameda County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,237,577 here, transfer tax runs about $19,925 at 16.10 dollars per thousand. Convention puts about $9,962 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $18,564.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly $183,865 in price and payment combined, and five years to $609,356.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

item.title: Park Avenue District, Emeryville: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Park Avenue District, Emeryville housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $429,369, up 0.03 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
The Park Avenue District is the old industrial heart of Emeryville, and the brick buildings are the reason it looks different from everything around it.

Emeryville incorporated in December 1896, on the second by the city's own account and the eighth by another, and it did it to protect a racetrack. Temescal residents had proposed a town that would have covered this ground too. That alarmed the business owners here, and a large part of the push to form a separate town was keeping the California Jockey Club track and the gambling revenue that came with it. The place is named for Joseph Emery, who arrived in the Gold Rush and bought land here. The city also built a large park around its shellmound in the late 1800s. The boundaries drawn by the founders in 1896 are substantially the ones in force today.

Emeryville has 8,497 housing units and 12.1 percent of them predate 1950. Only 5.8 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 24.2 percent, both the lowest in this entire series. The ACS median value is 604,800 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,936.

So this is a condominium and apartment market almost exclusively, and the building matters far more than the unit.

Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, because the reserve position is what turns into a special assessment. Ask what the association insures and what falls to you.

Ask directly whether the building has had a seismic retrofit and whether it is classified soft story, since lenders ask and a good deal of stock here sits over parking.

Ask whether there has been construction defect litigation. On attached housing this is a real question and the association minutes will show it.

Pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours. Emeryville is a small city with industrial roots and a lot of recent development, so what is permitted next door can differ sharply from what stands there now, and a view is not a protected asset.

Then pull the actual tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then stand on the street at nine on a weeknight. Emeryville empties differently from a residential city and you should know which version you are buying into.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Park Avenue District is $429,369 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.03 percent from the month before and down 6.3 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Emeryville for 2026-09. Active inventory is 70. 38 new listings came on, and 18 went pending. Median days on market is 36.

Median asking price is $585,194 at $530 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $429,369, up 0.03 percent month over month, down 6.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $4,572, or $54,860 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Emeryville I cover, and what each one is:

  • Bay Street. Bay Street is the retail centre of Emeryville and the housing built around it.
  • Doyle Hollis. Doyle and Hollis are the two streets this district is named for, in the middle of Emeryville.
  • East Baybridge. East BayBridge is the retail and housing development on Emeryville's southern edge, up against the Oakland line.
  • The Triangle. The Triangle is the residential pocket of Emeryville, and it is the part of the city that looks most like a neighborhood instead of a development.
  • Watergate. Watergate is the tower complex on Emeryville's bay edge, and it is unlike anything else in this series.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $4,572, $54,860 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. In Alameda County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 13.10 dollars per thousand, a $429,369 sale in Park Avenue District carries about $5,625 in transfer tax. It is normally split down the middle, about $2,812 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $1,000,000 the rate steps from 13.10 to 16.10 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $3,000 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $1,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $6,441.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near -$60,474. At five years it reaches -$166,249.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

The full report

The long version of this covers Park Avenue District, Emeryville in full, with the monthly tables, the financing detail, the property tax rules, cost of holding, programs, ADUs and every source dated. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/emeryville/park-avenue-district/.

item.title: Central Piedmont, Piedmont: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Central Piedmont, Piedmont housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $2,549,073, up 1.42 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Central Piedmont is the civic middle of a city that exists because of a sewer map.

Piedmont exists because Oakland was about to swallow it. When it became clear that Oakland, wanting the tax base, was preparing to annex this hill, a charter was drawn up in a hurry and Piedmont incorporated on January 30, 1907. The boundaries were taken off a sewer line map, and that is why the city's edges weave in and out of Oakland the way they do. It became a charter city on December 18, 1922, and voters adopted the charter on February 27, 1923.

Piedmont has 4,073 housing units and 71.7 percent of them predate 1950, the highest pre war share of any city in this series. 94.7 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 90.9 percent, both also the highest. The ACS median value tops out at the Census ceiling of 2,000,001 dollars and the city ZHVI is 2,549,073. Those three figures together describe something unusual: a city that is almost entirely owner occupied detached houses, most of them a century old.

So this is a pre war single family market with essentially no other product in it, and the inspection is the whole job.

Get a specialist inspection on anything pre 1930 and ask specifically about foundation bolting, because a large house on a hill that has never been bolted is both a structural and an insurance problem.

Then knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the sewer lateral, and the permit history on every addition. Houses of this size and age have usually been altered repeatedly and not all of that work was permitted.

Ask whether any local historic designation applies before you plan an exterior change.

On the sloped parcels, add the soils and drainage history, the condition and ownership of any retaining structures, and where water leaves the lot in a wet month.

Then confirm which city the parcel is actually in. Piedmont's boundary weaves through Oakland block by block, and city determines your school district, your transfer tax and your services. Take it from the assessor's parcel record, never from the mailing address.

What the market is doing right now

Central Piedmont sits at $2,549,073 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 1.42 percent since last month and up 14.6 percent since last year.

Realtor.com does not publish monthly listing metrics for Piedmont, so there is no inventory, days on market or asking price figure to report here. The value series above is measured separately and is unaffected.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $2,549,073, up 1.42 percent month over month, up 14.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $23,009, or $276,110 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Piedmont I cover, and what each one is:

  • Lower Piedmont. Lower Piedmont is the edge where the city meets Oakland, and in places the boundary runs down the middle of a block.
  • Upper Piedmont. Upper Piedmont is the top of the hill, and it has the largest houses and the longest views in the city.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $23,009 a month to own the typical home in Central Piedmont, $276,110 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 14.10 dollars per thousand, a $2,549,073 sale in Central Piedmont carries about $35,942 in transfer tax. It is normally split down the middle, about $17,971 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Emeryville at 26.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $63,727.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about $923,777 here. The five year figure is $3,474,044.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

The full report

item.content:encoded:
Lower Piedmont is the edge where the city meets Oakland, and in places the boundary runs down the middle of a block.

Piedmont exists because Oakland was about to swallow it. When it became clear that Oakland, wanting the tax base, was preparing to annex this hill, a charter was drawn up in a hurry and Piedmont incorporated on January 30, 1907. The boundaries were taken off a sewer line map, and that is why the city's edges weave in and out of Oakland the way they do. It became a charter city on December 18, 1922, and voters adopted the charter on February 27, 1923.

Piedmont has 4,073 housing units and 71.7 percent of them predate 1950, the highest pre war share of any city in this series. 94.7 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 90.9 percent, both also the highest. The ACS median value tops out at the Census ceiling of 2,000,001 dollars and the city ZHVI is 2,549,073. Those three figures together describe something unusual: a city that is almost entirely owner occupied detached houses, most of them a century old.

So this is a pre war single family market with essentially no other product in it, and the inspection is the whole job.

Get a specialist inspection on anything pre 1930 and ask specifically about foundation bolting, because a large house on a hill that has never been bolted is both a structural and an insurance problem.

Then knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, the sewer lateral, and the permit history on every addition. Houses of this size and age have usually been altered repeatedly and not all of that work was permitted.

item.content:encoded:
For twenty two years there was an amusement park at the end of this neighborhood, and people called it the Coney Island of the West.

Robert Strehlow opened Neptune Beach in 1917 on the waterfront that is now Crab Cove. Admission was a dime. There was a pool over three hundred feet long, a roller coaster, a hand carved carousel, barbecue pits, a clubhouse for dances, and high diving and steeplechase events. Ferries and the Southern Pacific brought the crowds in. The Depression, the new Bay Bridge and the shift to cars took the crowds away again, and the park closed in 1939. In 1940 they auctioned off the ferris wheel, the roller coaster and the carousel.

The year the park's rides were sold off, the Navy arrived. Naval Air Station Alameda was commissioned on November 1, 1940 at the west end of the island, and for the next fifty seven years the West End was a Navy neighborhood. Webster Street was its commercial spine. In the 1950s it ran to sailors, bars, all night restaurants and drive in theaters. The base closed in April 1997 and Webster Street lost its customer base in a single stroke. One longtime merchant put it plainly: the closure was good for Park Street and it killed Webster Street.

That history is still priced into this part of the island. The West End has the island's older and denser housing, more multi unit buildings, and a commercial street that has been rebuilding for almost thirty years.

What to do about it as a buyer. Check the year built and then check whether the building is one unit or several, because a lot of large single family houses on this side of Alameda were cut into flats during the Navy years and the conversion quality varies enormously. Pull the permit history on anything that looks converted. Then walk Webster Street on a weekday and again on a Saturday. The direction this corridor is moving is the single biggest variable in what a West End house is worth in ten years, and you can read it better standing on the sidewalk than in a spreadsheet.

Central Alameda is the part of the island everybody drives through and nobody can draw the boundary of.

The sources genuinely disagree. One puts it between Park Street and Grand Avenue, bounded by the estuary and Central Avenue. Many of those buildings predate the city charter rules that voters passed in 1973 banning new multifamily construction, tightened in 1991 with a density cap of one unit per 2,000 square feet of land. A repeal went on the ballot in 2020 and failed.

So the legal unit count is the first question on any purchase here, not the last. Get the permit history, confirm with the city that every unit is legal and not an unpermitted 1940s conversion, and ask whether the building is nonconforming, because nonconforming status limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects both financing and insurance.

There was a seventy room mansion on Fernside Boulevard and it burned to the ground in 1897 with nobody in it.

It belonged to Alfred A. Cohen, and the money that built it came from the railroad. Cohen built the San Francisco and Alameda Railroad in 1864, the same line whose Alameda stop created the commercial district at Lincoln and Park. In 1868 he sold his railroads and his ferries to the Central Pacific's Big Four, and he put the proceeds into an estate here on the east end of the island. Sources put the estate at somewhere between about 102 and 250 acres. The house went up in flames in March 1897. Accounts differ on whether it was the twenty third or the twenty fourth, and one source puts the fire a year later, though 1897 is the better supported date.

The neighborhood came out of the estate's breakup. Emilie Cohen died in 1924, her children sold the land to a developer named Fred Wood, and Wood laid out the streets that are there now. A separate project, Fernside Marina, went in along the estuary in 1938 and is generally described as the last subdivision on Alameda's estuary shoreline.

So the housing here is 1920s and newer, Craftsman and bungalow through mid century, on a layout more generous than the old grid closer to town. A remnant of the original subdivision survives in the neighborhood's homeowners association, and that is unusual for ground of this age.

Fernside also runs along the tidal canal, the 1902 cut that severed this peninsula from Oakland and made Alameda an island. The Fruitvale and High Street bridges cross it here, and that is both the appeal and the thing to check. This is the shortest way off the island toward the freeway, and it is also the closest you can live to a drawbridge.

Three things before you write an offer. Confirm whether the address is inside the association and read what it governs, because an association tied to a 1920s subdivision can carry restrictions nobody raises at an open house. Pull the year built, since a 1920s bungalow and a 1950s house are different inspection problems entirely. On this side of the island that premium moves a monthly payment more than a quarter point of rate does.

The name is not marketing. It is what people started calling these blocks when the money moved in during the late 1800s, and the Victorian and Edwardian houses that got built are still standing in rows.

The first wave came before the streetcar. The second came right after it, when the Alameda, Oakland and Piedmont electric line arrived in 1892 and made a daily commute possible from a neighborhood of large lots. Local historians treat that post 1892 stretch as the classic phase here. William Farragut Chipman, son of one of Alameda's founders, was behind the King Street Opening tract the same year.

What that produced is one of the denser concentrations of intact nineteenth century residential architecture anywhere in the Bay Area, on a street grid that was laid out for carriages and never widened.

What to understand about buying one. These houses are the reason people move to Alameda and they are also the most expensive houses in the city to maintain, in a way that does not show up until you own one. Original wood windows, original siding, decorative exterior millwork, and in many cases knob and tube wiring and galvanized supply lines still in service. None of that is a reason to walk. It is the reason the gap between a restored house and an original one on the same block runs into six figures.

So do this. Get a specialist inspection, not a general one, on anything built before 1910, and ask specifically about the foundation and whether the house has ever been bolted. Ask for the permit history, because a lot of work on these houses was done without one. Find out whether the property sits inside any local historic designation and what that means for exterior changes before you plan a renovation. A second measure in 1991 capped density citywide at one unit per 2,000 square feet of land. A repeal went on the 2020 ballot and failed. The practical effect is that many of the multi unit buildings here predate the ban, so they exist legally but could not be built again today.

item.content:encoded:
Bethlehem Steel built ships on this ground from 1916 to 1948. Joseph Seiger and Michael Humphreys put the Marina Village complex up on it afterward.

That is the short version of Alameda's north shore. The strip along Clement Avenue facing the Oakland and Alameda estuary was industrial waterfront for most of the twentieth century, and the adjacent Alameda Marina site, roughly 44 acres of it, has run as an industrial boating and marine craft maintenance and storage operation since 1950. Some of that work is still there, mixed in with light industrial and professional tenants.

The site has been in play for two decades. In 2005 the owner, Pacific Shops Inc., wanted to sell. The Svendsen family formed a partnership to pursue it, and Bay West Development Group was later brought in to seek entitlements for mixed use and multifamily redevelopment. The city has designated the Alameda Marina site for mixed use redevelopment after a public process.

So this is the part of Alameda where the next large scale change is most likely to happen, and that is the single most important thing to understand before you buy here.

That is also the practical instruction. Go to the city and read the current entitlements and plans for the Alameda Marina site and for the parcels around any address you are considering. These are public documents, the process has been running for years, and what gets approved will change your view, your traffic and your value. That matters more here than the condition of any individual kitchen.

Then the ordinary work. Much of the housing on this side is attached or inside an association, so get the budget and the reserve study, not just the dues. Ask what the association insures. This is low ground on the estuary, so get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire, and ask the inspector about settlement and about the condition of any seawall or bulkhead the property depends on.

And remember the city charter. Alameda voters banned new multifamily construction in 1973 and capped density in 1991, and a 2020 repeal failed, so what can be built here is a live legal question and not a settled one.

item.title: Bay Farm, Alameda: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Bay Farm, Alameda housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,145,869, up 0.59 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
A man named Amos Mecartney tried to farm this ground in the 1870s and it did not work out. Mecartney Road is still named after him.

Bay Farm Island is the part of Alameda that is not on the main island, and most of what you can stand on today was put there on purpose. Utah Construction's landfill project added roughly 940 acres here, converting marshland and tidelands, with about 600 acres going to Harbor Bay Isle and the balance to the Harbor Bay Business Park. By Utah's own 1968 report to shareholders the dredge had placed 22 million yards of fill at Bay Farm.

Development arrived in stages before the master plan did. Through the 1950s and 1960s, developers bought out the families who still held land here, and Braddock and Logan built the townhouse communities of Garden Isle, Casitas and Islandia. The bigger plan came in 1972, when Utah and Ron Cowan's Doric Development formed Harbor Bay Isle Associates.

What it means in practice. Bay Farm is the newest housing in Alameda, it is overwhelmingly planned development with associations attached, and it is the only part of the city where you are driving instead of walking to a commercial street. It is also where Oakland's airport sits immediately to the south.

So go listen before you commit. Stand at the specific address at different times of day, because aircraft noise varies by flight path and by hour and no listing will characterize it for you. Then handle the three questions that apply to everything out here: get the association's reserve study and budget instead of just the dues number, ask your inspector specifically about settlement on fill, and get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire. Those three answers will change your monthly cost more than anything you can negotiate on price.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Bay Farm is $1,145,869: up 0.59 percent against last month, up 2.1 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Alameda for 2026-09. Active inventory is 71. 42 new listings came on, and 29 went pending. Median days on market is 34.

Median asking price is $972,000 at $617 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,145,869, up 0.59 percent month over month, up 2.1 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $10,804, or $129,647 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Alameda I cover, and what each one is:

  • Alameda Point. This is 1,560 acres of the island that belonged to the United States Navy until 1997, and the Secretary of the Interior made the heart of it a National Historic Landmark District in January 2013.
  • Ballena Bay. Ballena Bay is an island off the side of an island, and a good part of it runs on a lease from the city.
  • Bronze Coast. The Bronze Coast sits between the Gold Coast and the rest of the island, and the name tells you exactly what it is: the same era, a step down in scale.
  • Central Alameda. Central Alameda is the part of the island everybody drives through and nobody can draw the boundary of.
  • Fernside. There was a seventy room mansion on Fernside Boulevard and it burned to the ground in 1897 with nobody in it.
  • Gold Coast. The name is not marketing.
  • Harbor Bay Isle. Harbor Bay Isle was supposed to be ten thousand homes.
  • Harbor Bay. Harbor Bay is the half of the Bay Farm fill that was built for work instead of for living, and the ferry is the reason anyone commutes from it.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Bay Farm home and the monthly carry lands near $10,804. That is $129,647 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Bay Farm home, $1,145,869, comes to roughly $15,011 at a rate of 13.10 per thousand. Convention puts about $7,505 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,188.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $56,488, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $175,964.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $6,679 monthly, or $80,145 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

item.description: What the Downtown Hayward, Hayward housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $816,424, up 0.13 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
The city was incorporated on March 11, 1876 under the name Haywards, with the s, and it was named after a hotel.

That hotel was the landmark the town had grown around, and downtown is still where the grid is oldest and tightest. The commercial spine runs along B Street and Mission Boulevard, and the Hayward BART station sits at the edge of it. That is the practical reason downtown prices differently from the rest of the city.

What built Hayward was fruit. From the second half of the nineteenth century this was one of California's leading fruit growing areas, sending cherries, apricots, peaches, tomatoes and potatoes out by rail. Hunt Brothers opened a cannery here in 1895 and ran it as a seasonal industry substantial enough to build cottages and community buildings around itself. By 1950 the city had about 14,000 residents and was calling itself the Apricot City. After the Second World War the orchards went under housing tracts.

Hayward has 52,243 housing units and only 9.1 percent of them predate 1950, so this is overwhelmingly a postwar city. 51.2 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 58.0 percent, the ACS median value is 854,400 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,391. Downtown is where the pre 1950 share is highest and where most of the multi unit stock sits.

So the questions here are the older and denser ones.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, because conversions happen in older downtown stock and not all of them were permitted. Get the permit history. Ask whether the building is nonconforming, since that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and affects financing and insurance.

On pre war buildings, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring and galvanized supply lines.

Then the fault. The Hayward Fault runs along the base of these hills and through this city, so ask for any seismic report on the property and whether the house has ever been bolted to its foundation. That question matters more in Hayward than in most places.

Then walk from the address to the BART platform and time it. That walk is what the downtown premium buys.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Downtown Hayward home is worth $816,424. That is up 0.13 percent on the month and down 2.4 percent on the year.

Listing activity in Hayward for 2026-09. Active inventory is 194. 96 new listings came on, and 78 went pending. Median days on market is 42.

Median asking price is $829,716 at $553 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $816,424, up 0.13 percent month over month, down 2.4 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,938, or $95,260 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Hayward I cover, and what each one is:

  • Burbank. Burbank is one of Hayward's older central neighborhoods, close in to downtown, and the published history belongs to the city, not the pocket, so this is that history plus the development record.
  • Eden Shores. Eden Shores is the newest ground in Hayward and it sits out on the bay edge.
  • Fairview Hills. Fairview Hills is on the unincorporated slope above Hayward, and that word unincorporated is the practical headline.
  • Fairway Park. Fairway Park is postwar Hayward out toward the bay side, laid out around a golf course, and the name is literal.
  • Glen Eden. Eden is the old name for this whole area.
  • Harder Tennyson. Harder and Tennyson are the two roads this neighborhood is named for, in the southern part of Hayward, and the history here is the city's.
  • Hayward Highland. Hayward Highland sits on the slope above the city with the Hayward Fault running along the foot of it.
  • Hayward Hills. The Hayward Fault runs along the base of these hills, and it is the reason there are hills here at all.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $7,938 monthly, or $95,260 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Alameda County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $816,424 here, transfer tax runs about $7,838 at 9.60 dollars per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $3,919 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $12,246.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$44,655 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$130,051.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

item.description: What the Mt Eden, Hayward housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $940,793, down 0.25 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
In 1918 a man named Zenjuro Shibata moved out from Oakland and started a nursery here. California law at the time barred him from holding the land in his own name, so the purchase was recorded in his eldest son Yoshio's.

Mt. Eden Nursery began on a marshy plot that flooded, growing vegetables and flowers. The first greenhouse went up that same year, 1918, planted in carnations. In the mid 1930s the family switched the main crop to roses. During the Second World War the Shibatas were removed to Tule Lake. The nursery came back afterward and kept operating into the 1980s, and the greenhouses were finally demolished in the 1990s.

What is left is the garden. The Shibata Garden at 25941 Industrial Boulevard is the surviving piece of the Mt. Eden Nursery Company, and it is on this neighborhood's ground.

Mt. Eden was its own township before Hayward grew around it, out on the flat western side of the city toward the bay. The land that grew flowers and vegetables is now a mix of housing and industrial ground.

There is a cemetery at Post Street and Bonde Way that is older than the city around it by a century.

Centerville Pioneer Cemetery goes back to 1855, when the Alameda Presbyterian Church, organized two years earlier, bought the ground under the Reverend William Wallace Brier and nine other founding members. California recognized it as a state cemetery in 1859 and it went into the California Register of Historic Resources in 1976. The names in it are the names on the road signs. Herman Eggers is buried there. So is Blacow, and Blacow Road still runs through this part of Fremont.

That is the useful thing to understand about Centerville. It was one of five separate townships, with Mission San Jose, Niles, Irvington and Warm Springs, and all five voted to become one city on January 23, 1956. Washington Township had organized the area as far back as 1853. Newark was invited into the merger and its voters said no. Newark is a separate city today and incorporated on its own in 1955. Centerville was a town with a main street before Fremont existed, and the commercial spine along Fremont Boulevard and Peralta Boulevard is the remains of it.

What that means on the ground. The housing here is older and denser than the tract neighborhoods east of it, with a mix that includes genuine pre war stock, post war infill and apartment buildings along the arterials. It is also the part of Fremont closest to the Centerville train station. For anyone commuting south that is a real factor.

If you are looking here, do two things. Pull the year built on every address you are serious about, because the range on a single street can be fifty years and the inspection list is completely different at either end. Then go stand at the Centerville station during the evening commute. Rail access is most of why people pay to be on this side of Fremont, and whether the schedule actually fits your day is something you can settle in one trip instead of after you move.

  • Baylands. This is the edge of Fremont where the city stops and the bay starts, and most of it is federally protected.
  • Brookvale. Brookvale is one of the Fremont neighborhoods where the published history is genuinely thin, so this is the development record and the practical read, not a story somebody made up.

  • Glenmoor. Glenmoor has a homeowners association that was incorporated in March 1953, when there were no more than 75 houses standing in the whole subdivision.
  • Grimmer. Grimmer is named for a family nobody has documented properly, and the honest thing is to say so.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $8,931 a month to own the typical home in Centerville, $107,170 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

item.title: Mission San Jose, Fremont: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Mission San Jose, Fremont housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $2,140,736, up 0.36 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
The oldest standing adobe building in Alameda County is in this neighborhood, and it has been there since 1809.

Old Mission San Jose sits at 43300 Mission Boulevard, at the Washington Boulevard intersection. The mission was founded on June 11, 1797, the fourteenth in Alta California. The 1868 earthquake took down the adobe church and most of what stood around it. The building that survived is the one from 1809, originally the padres living quarters and now the museum. The church you see is a reconstruction, begun in 1981 and finished in 1985, built with period materials and period methods, not a modern frame behind a facade.

Go into the garden. The olive trees in it are roughly two hundred years old and date to the mission period, and the mission orchards once supplied oil and fruit well beyond this valley. A town grew up around the mission with its own post office from 1850, and grapes, nursery plants and olives carried the local economy for decades before anyone subdivided anything.

The land reads the same way today. This is the eastern edge of Fremont where the valley floor runs up into the hills, so the lots on the uphill side sit higher and look back across the bay, and the streets bend to follow the grade instead of running on a grid.

What you are buying here. A mix that runs from mission era ground through mid century tracts to much newer infill. Two houses four blocks apart can be forty years apart in construction type. item.content:encoded:
Charlie Chaplin made five pictures on one block of Niles Boulevard, and you can still sit in a building there and watch them.

Gilbert Anderson, who the country knew as Broncho Billy, went looking for somewhere with mild winters and country that read as the West on film. He picked Niles. Construction on the full Essanay studio began in 1913 to a design by George W. Page, two hundred feet long and fifty wide, with a glass enclosed stage to catch the daylight, Western street sets, and a horse stable behind. Chaplin shot his first Essanay picture in Chicago and came out here for the rest. The Tramp, 1915, was his sixth film for the company and the fifth he made in Niles. A Night Out came out that February and The Champion in March. He left for Mutual in 1916 and the studio was finished by 1918.

The Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum is at 37417 Niles Boulevard, in the Edison Theater, a century old nickelodeon a short walk from where the studio stood. They run silent programs with live accompaniment. Go once, on a weekend, and the street stops reading as a quiet commercial strip.

The older thing in Niles is the canyon. Niles Canyon carried the final stretch of the First Transcontinental Railroad, and the eleven mile section between Sunol and Niles went on the National Register in October 2010 as the Niles Canyon Transcontinental Railroad Historic District. The Pacific Locomotive Association leased the right of way and started rebuilding track in 1987. The first passenger train ran from Sunol in May 1988, and it still runs.

What that means for a house here. Niles is the one part of Fremont with a genuine pre war main street, and the housing around it is older and smaller than the tract stock that covers most of the city. Expect pre war construction and the inspection items that come with it. Leland Stanford bought a resort here in 1869 and his brother turned it into a winery that held half a million gallons.

Josiah Stanford ran the operation and built the vineyard out to 350 acres, with winery capacity around 500,000 gallons. The site is California Historical Landmark 642. Most of that ground is housing now and a single brick building is what is left. That is the usual ending for Bay Area agriculture, though not usually this close to a BART platform. The Weibel name on the neighborhood immediately north is the next chapter of the same story, a champagne operation that worked the Stanford site after the Stanfords.

The other thing about Warm Springs is the plant at the south end of Fremont. General Motors broke ground on Fremont Assembly in September 1961 and the first car came off the line in May 1963. GM closed it in 1982. It reopened in 1984 as NUMMI, a joint venture between GM and Toyota that rehired about 85 percent of the laid off workforce and then produced more than eight million vehicles, peaking at 428,633 in 2006. Toyota shut it in April 2010 and roughly 4,700 people lost their jobs. Tesla bought it at a steep discount and reopened it that October. In 2023 it built close to 560,000 vehicles and employed more than twenty thousand people.

That matters here in a way it does not matter in most neighborhoods. Two large employers inside two decades, with a hard stop in between, is the local economic history, and the housing demand in south Fremont tracks it.

That house is still standing, and it is the reason this neighborhood has a name that sounds like an estate. Patterson had reached Alameda County by 1851 and kept buying land. In 1889 the family brought in Samuel Newsom, one of the better known Victorian architects working in California, and wrapped the plain farmhouse in a Queen Anne addition. Three generations of Pattersons lived in it. In 1984 the family gave 131 acres at the center of the property to the City of Fremont, and since 1985 the East Bay Regional Park District has run it as a working farm kept at its turn of the century condition.

Ardenwood Historic Farm is the result. Draft horses, crops, a narrow gauge train, and docents in period clothing running tours of the Patterson House on Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays during the season. It is the best hour you can spend with a kid in this city, and most people in Fremont have never gone.

The neighborhood around it is a different era entirely. This is Fremont's northwest corner, laid out late and built out as planned subdivision, so the housing stock is newer and more uniform than anywhere in the historic districts, with a lot of it inside homeowner associations. The Dumbarton Bridge approach is right here. That is the whole reason a certain kind of buyer looks at Ardenwood first. this is the Fremont neighborhood with the shortest drive to the Peninsula.

So buy it for that, but verify it. Drive the bridge at eight in the morning on a Tuesday before you commit, because the approach backs up and the map time is not the real time. The Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1972 after years of local campaigning against the filling of the bayfront. Arthur Ogilvie helped organize the committee that pushed for it. Congress named the refuge for Congressman Don Edwards in 1995, and the Fremont visitor center opened in 1979. Mowry Slough, in Fremont, is inside the refuge. One source gives the founding year as 1974, but the Fish and Wildlife Service and the Federal Register both say 1972.

That history is the whole character of the Baylands. The reason there is open tidal marsh at the end of Fremont instead of more subdivision is that people fought to keep it, and then the federal government took it on.

So there is very little housing out here, and that is the first thing to understand if you are searching the Baylands. What people usually mean is the newer development inland of the marsh instead of anything on it. Fremont has 81,579 housing units in total and about 2 percent predate 1950, so what exists on this side is recent, planned, and often inside an association.

Three things to establish on a specific address. Get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire, because this is low flat ground at the bay margin and the premium is a real monthly number, not a closing detail. Ask the inspector about settlement and look hard at foundations and flatwork, since ground near filled marsh behaves differently from ground on the valley floor. And on anything in a homeowners association, read the reserve study, not just the dues.

item.description: What the Brookvale, Fremont housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,767,875, down 0.12 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Brookvale is one of the Fremont neighborhoods where the published history is genuinely thin, so this is the development record and the practical read, not a story somebody made up.

What the sources say, and they disagree, is that Brookvale filled in later than the 1950s and 1960s tracts, with one guide putting much of the housing in the 1970s and 1980s as demand spread south from the bay and north from Silicon Valley. Treat the decade as approximate until somebody checks the tract maps at the county. For context, the five townships of Centerville, Irvington, Mission San Jose, Niles and Warm Springs voted to become one city on January 23, 1956, so anything built here in the 1970s went up into a city that was already twenty years old and filling in its last open ground.

The sourced figures are the city's and they are solid. On September 6, 1960 the Fremont City Council picked the Fudenna ranch as the site for its civic center. The city was four years old and it was choosing where its middle would be.

What got built there is the reason this neighborhood exists. Central Park started development in 1960. The Hub shopping center opened in October 1962. The city government building went up in 1968. Lake Elizabeth was created in 1968 by excavating part of Stivers Lagoon Marsh, and the city dedicated it on March 22, 1969 to its sister city, Elizabeth in Australia. The lake runs 82 acres inside 174 acres that Alameda County Flood Control leases to the city on condition it stays park and recreation land. Central Park is around 450 acres now and the paved loop around the lake is about two miles.

One detail worth knowing. Stivers Lagoon is one of a chain of freshwater marshes strung along the east side of the Hayward Fault. The lake is where it is because the fault put water there.

Glenmoor has a homeowners association that was incorporated in March 1953, when there were no more than 75 houses standing in the whole subdivision. It was probably the first one in the Fremont area, and it predates the city of Fremont by three years.

The developer was Glenmoor Homes, Inc., formed in 1951 by James R. Meyer with the civil engineer Ralph E. Cotter Jr., the contractors James L. and Robert H. Before that it was farms. Seven large ones covered this ground, and the family names on them are the names you now drive on and look up in the Centerville cemetery: Garrett Norris, Herman Eggers, Robert Blacow, Martin Brophy, Ashley Cameron.

What it is now is the clearest example of a postwar ranch neighborhood in central Fremont. Single story, generous lots by Bay Area standards, wide streets, and two parks the association still runs, Meyer Park and Alta Park.

That consistency is the thing to use. Because 1,900 houses went up from one developer inside fifteen years, the comparable sales here are genuinely comparable. That is rare, and it makes pricing unusually readable. item.content:encoded:
This neighborhood is named after a chicken farm and a school board member, and the chicken farm was world famous.

John E. Kimber started Kimber Farms at Niles in 1925. The detailed company history puts the starting flock at 800 hens, though a local museum exhibit says 80,000, so take the smaller figure as the better documented one. Kimber was born in New York in 1895 and came out of Stanford in 1917 with a major in agriculture and a minor in music. The farm lost money for seven straight years and turned its first profit in 1932. Then it did something almost nobody in the industry was doing: it hired a full time geneticist, becoming only the second poultry breeder anywhere to employ one. Accounts differ on the year, with the company history saying 1934 and another source naming Dr W. F. Lamoreux in 1943. It also put a veterinarian on part time to autopsy every bird that died so the cause could be traced through each family line.

Kimber Farms incorporated on December 3, 1946, with Niles as headquarters and operations at Atascadero, Los Gatos, Sanger and Clovis. Its 1955 catalogue was about building a more profitable White Leghorn. By the 1940s through the 1960s the operation had international standing, and the USDA's National Agricultural Library holds its records today.

The Gomes half honors John Gomes, from a pioneer farming family that worked the fields nearby. He sat on the Irvington School Board for years and served as a director of the Alameda County Water District. John Gomes Elementary was built for the Way Out West and Mission Valley housing, took its first students in September 1969 and was dedicated in March 1970. The building is a six sided pod design and it still looks like nothing else around it.

So the housing here is late 1960s and after, built on former farm and ranch ground. That is the Fremont pattern. Only about 2 percent of the city's stock predates 1950.

Pull the year built and the lot dimensions. On single story houses of this era with generous lots, check setbacks early if an ADU is in your plan. Then go look at the Gomes pod building. You will not mistake it for anything else.

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $21,556, $258,670 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

item.content:encoded:
The name on this neighborhood came off a wine label.

Weibel Champagne Vineyards worked the ground at the old Leland Stanford winery site in Warm Springs, immediately south of here. Stanford bought that resort property in 1869 and his brother Josiah built the vineyard out to 350 acres with winery capacity around half a million gallons. The site is California Historical Landmark 642. When the Stanford era ended, Weibel's operation carried it on, and the Weibel name ended up on the hillside neighborhood and on its school.

Fred E. Weibel Elementary was built in 1987 at the foot of Mission Peak. The building was designed for its slope, with ramps and paths running with the grade and drought resistant planting along them. That tells you most of what you need to know about the terrain.

Because this is hillside ground on the eastern edge of Fremont, the housing is newer and the lots are cut into grade. Across the city only about 2 percent of the 81,579 housing units predate 1950, and up here essentially none of it does. The views are west across the bay and they are the reason for the price.

So shop it as a hill purchase, because that is what it is. Ask for the soils and drainage history on the specific parcel, since on a sloped lot the ground is the expensive part and a retaining wall is not a cosmetic item. Have the inspector look specifically at drainage, at any retaining structures, and at how water leaves the property in a wet month. Ask whether the house has ever been bolted to its foundation.

Then get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire, and ask the broker to explain the risk rating. Hillside ground against open space on the east side of Fremont prices differently from the flats and you want that number early.

And drive up to the Mission Peak trailhead once on a weekend morning. The parking situation at the trailhead is a genuine part of living on these streets.

What the market is doing right now

  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Fremont I cover, and what each one is:

  • Ardenwood. A Pennsylvania farmer named George Washington Patterson came to California for gold in 1849, found almost none, and in 1857 built a redwood farmhouse here instead.
  • Baylands. This is the edge of Fremont where the city stops and the bay starts, and most of it is federally protected.
  • Brookvale. Brookvale is one of the Fremont neighborhoods where the published history is genuinely thin, so this is the development record and the practical read, not a story somebody made up.
  • Cabrillo. Cabrillo is a 1960s tract neighborhood in north Fremont, and the useful facts about it are in the development record instead of in any story.
  • Centerville. There is a cemetery at Post Street and Bonde Way that is older than the city around it by a century.

item.title: Old Town Newark, Newark: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Old Town Newark, Newark housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,185,129, down 0.08 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Newark exists as a separate city because its chamber of commerce did not want to be the industrial zone of somebody else's town.

Newark is named after a castle in Scotland. J. Barr Robertson gave it the name, taken from Newark Castle at Port Glasgow. A company bought the land from Washington Township in 1878 to lay the town out, and before that, in 1853, Mayhew's Landing here held warehouses for wheat, hay and coal. The city came much later and it came by refusal: when the five townships around it were merging into Fremont, Newark's Chamber of Commerce objected to being zoned mainly for industry inside that new city and pushed to incorporate on its own instead. Newark became a city on September 22, 1955, the first new city in Alameda County in 47 years. Fremont incorporated four months later, in January 1956, without it.

Old Town is the original grid from the 1878 layout and it is where whatever pre war stock the city has sits.

Newark has 16,015 housing units and 4.5 percent of them predate 1950. 67.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 69.4 percent, the ACS median value is 1,142,800 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,776.

So pull the year built, because Old Town is the one part of Newark where a genuinely old house is plausible.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing and get the permit history.

On pre war stock: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of original windows and siding. Ask whether any local historic designation applies before planning an exterior change.

Then the ground. Newark sits on the flat bay side of the county, so get the flood zone determination with a written insurance quote before your contingencies expire and ask the inspector about settlement.

Then check the zoning on the parcel and its neighbours, because the whole reason this city exists is a disagreement about industrial zoning and industrial ground still sits close to housing here.

Then walk the old grid. A town laid out in 1878 that refused to be absorbed in 1955 is a more interesting place than its reputation suggests.

What the market is doing right now

$1,185,129 is the typical Old Town Newark home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is down 0.08 percent, and over the year down 2.4 percent.

  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Newark I cover, and what each one is:

  • Birch Grove. Birch Grove is a postwar Newark neighborhood on the city's flat ground.
  • Bridgepointe. Bridgepointe is one of Newark's later planned developments.
  • Cherry Thornton. Cherry and Thornton are the two streets this Newark neighborhood is named for.
  • Lakeshore. Lakeshore is one of Newark's planned residential neighborhoods, laid out around water features on the flat bay side of the city.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Old Town Newark home and the monthly carry lands near $11,145. That is $133,745 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Alameda County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Old Town Newark charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,185,129 home owes roughly $1,304 at transfer. Custom is to split it, so about $652 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,777.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near -$64,164. At five years it reaches -$186,938.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

West Dublin is the older half of a city that is itself only incorporated since February 1982.

Jose Maria Amador received over 16,000 acres here in 1835 for his service as a Mexican soldier and as administrator at Mission San Jose, and the Amador Valley carries his name. Put the minimum down on the typical West Dublin home and the monthly carry lands near $11,516. That is $138,189 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

Dublin Ranch is the largest of the master planned communities that turned east Dublin from open land into a suburb.

The valley's record starts with a land grant. James Witt Dougherty then bought 10,000 acres from Amador and became the largest landowner in the area. None of that touched this ground directly. The eastern side of the valley stayed open until the city, incorporated only in February 1982, began approving large scale development on it.

Dublin has 25,157 housing units and 0.8 percent of them predate 1950, among the lowest shares of any city in this series. 54.2 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 65.7 percent, the ACS median value is 1,317,100 dollars and the median gross rent is 3,191. Dublin Ranch is squarely in that recent cohort: planned layout, consistent housing, homeowners associations throughout, and a golf course at its centre.

So the association and the tax bill come before the house.

Get the association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, because the reserve position is what becomes a special assessment. Ask what it insures, what it maintains, and whether any of that includes slopes, drainage or private roads.

Then pull the actual tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate. Development of this era in Dublin frequently sits inside a community facilities district, and those assessments ride on top of the base rate. Then the house. On stock this recent the list is the roof, the water heater, the furnace and the air conditioning, plus any original dual pane windows, because those are the systems that reach end of life first.

Ask what is entitled on the parcels around you, because east Dublin has been building continuously and an open field is not a permanent view.

Then drive the commute at your real hour, and check the BART park and ride situation if you intend to use it, because that is the constraint people underestimate here.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Dublin Ranch home at $1,227,704 on 2026-09-30, down 0.36 percent month over month and down 5.5 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,262,500 at $628 per square foot.

Inside it

  • Downtown Dublin. The oldest things in Dublin sit at the corner of Dublin Boulevard and Donlon Way, and there are three of them.
  • East Dublin. East Dublin is the reason this city grew from a crossroads to a suburb inside one generation.
  • Fallon Village. Fallon Village carries the name of Jeremiah Fallon, who arrived in this valley in 1846 and bought 982 acres from Jose Maria Amador in the 1850s with Gold Rush money.
  • Jordan Ranch. Jordan Ranch is one of the named communities in east Dublin, developed as part of the city's continuing eastern build out.
  • Positano. Positano is one of the master planned villages on Dublin's eastern side, built as part of the city's recent expansion.
  • Schaefer Ranch. Schaefer Ranch sits on the western hillside edge of Dublin, above the freeway, and it is one of the city's later developments.
  • Tassajara Hills. Tassajara Hills sits on the rising ground at Dublin's northeastern edge, where the city runs up against open hills.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $11,516 a month, $138,189 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$151,741 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$422,060.

item.description: What the Downtown Pleasanton, Pleasanton housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,500,493, down 0.01 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
The town is spelled wrong on purpose, or at least it has been since 1894.

Pleasanton incorporated on June 18, 1894 and took its name from Major General Alfred Pleasonton of the Union Army. His name has an o in the middle. The town's does not, and the misspelling stuck.

Before that it was Alisal, a mercantile stop on the Gold Rush road in the 1850s. The ground was Rancho el Valle de San Jose, granted in 1839 to the Bernal brothers and their brothers-in-law. In 1858 the Bernal family built a one-mile racetrack here, and it is still the oldest in the country. John Kottinger is credited by most historians with founding the town proper: the railroad was announced in 1862, he started selling plots along the planned route the next year, and by 1869 there was a town and the transcontinental line running through it. Kottinger also established what one history calls the first commercial vineyards and winery in Alameda County, in the 1850s. At one point Pleasanton was among the largest hop producers in the world.

Main Street downtown is the survivor of all of that, and it is one of the better intact small commercial streets in the East Bay.

Pleasanton has 28,975 housing units and only 2.5 percent of them predate 1950. 61.1 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 67.0 percent, the ACS median value is 1,537,100 dollars and the median gross rent is 3,060. Downtown carries almost all of the city's pre war stock and most of what multi unit housing there is.

So pull the year built, because downtown is the one part of Pleasanton where a genuinely old house is likely.

On pre war stock: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the permit history on every addition. Ask whether the property carries any local historic designation before you plan an exterior change.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city on anything that may hold more than one household.

Then do a Saturday on foot from the front door. Main Street is the premium here and you should test it with your own legs.

What the market is doing right now

$1,500,493 is the typical Downtown Pleasanton home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is down 0.01 percent, and over the year down 3.0 percent.

Median asking price is $1,433,972 at $735 per square foot.

  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,888, or $166,662 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Pleasanton I cover, and what each one is:

  • Birdland. Birdland takes its name from its streets.
  • Del Prado. Del Prado is a postwar Pleasanton tract and its published history is the city's, so this is that plus the development record.
  • Golden Eagle. Golden Eagle sits on the hillside ground at the edge of Pleasanton, built late and built large.
  • Kottinger Ranch. This neighborhood is named for the man who sold the first lots in Pleasanton.
  • Laguna Oaks. Laguna Oaks is one of Pleasanton's later hillside developments, built large on big lots.
  • Mohr Martin. Mohr and Martin are the two roads this neighborhood is named for, on the flatter western side of Pleasanton.
  • Pleasanton Meadows. Pleasanton Meadows is a postwar tract on the valley floor and the name is as literal as it sounds.
  • Ruby Hill. Ruby Hill is a gated development on vineyard ground, and the vineyard part is older than almost anything else in this valley.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $13,888, $166,662 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Alameda County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 1.10 dollars per thousand, a $1,500,493 sale in Downtown Pleasanton carries about $1,651 in transfer tax. It is normally split down the middle, about $825 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Emeryville at 26.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $37,512.

item.content:encoded:
Ruby Hill is a gated development on vineyard ground, and the vineyard part is older than almost anything else in this valley.

Ruby Hill is the modern chapter: a large planned community on the eastern side of the city with a winery name and a golf course at its centre.

Pleasanton has 28,975 housing units and only 2.5 percent of them predate 1950. 61.1 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 67.0 percent, the ACS median value is 1,537,100 dollars and the median gross rent is 3,060. So the association is the first thing you are buying, alongside the house.

Get the budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, because the reserve position is what becomes a special assessment. Ask what the association maintains, what it insures, and what the gate and road obligations are, since private roads inside a gated community are a real long term cost.

Read the governing documents on what is enforced, because a development of this type generally has detailed architectural rules and they will apply to anything you want to change.

Then pull the actual tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, because planned development of this era frequently carries community facilities district assessments on top of the base rate and they can be substantial.

Ruby Hill charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,500,493 home owes roughly $1,651 at transfer. Convention puts about $825 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

item.content:encoded:
This neighborhood is named for the man who sold the first lots in Pleasanton.

John Kottinger is credited by most historians with founding the town. The railroad was announced in 1862, Kottinger began selling plots along the planned route in 1863, and by 1869 there was a town with the transcontinental line running through it. He is also credited with establishing the first commercial vineyards and winery in Alameda County here in the 1850s. Before any of that the ground was Rancho el Valle de San Jose, granted in 1839 to the Bernal brothers and their brothers-in-law, and the settlement was called Alisal, a mercantile stop on the Gold Rush road.

Kottinger Ranch is the hillside ground above town carrying his name, developed late and built large.

Pleasanton has 28,975 housing units and only 2.5 percent of them predate 1950. 61.1 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 67.0 percent, the ACS median value is 1,537,100 dollars and the median gross rent is 3,060. Up here the lots are bigger, the houses are newer and larger than the citywide figures suggest, and the ground is sloped.

So this is a hillside purchase and the questions follow from that.

Ask for the soils and drainage history on the specific parcel. Ask who owns and maintains any retaining structures and what condition they are in, because a failing retaining wall is the most expensive surprise on a hill lot and it is frequently a shared obligation. Ask the inspector where water leaves the property in a wet month.

Get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire, with the risk rating explained, since this is hill ground against open space on the valley's edge.

If the property sits inside a homeowners association, get the budget and the reserve study, not the dues number, and ask specifically what the association maintains on the slopes.

Then pull the actual tax bill for the address, because hillside development of this era frequently carries district assessments on top of the base rate.
