item.title: Downtown Livermore, Livermore: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Downtown Livermore, Livermore housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,071,869, up 0.03 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Livermore was platted and registered on November 4, 1869, and the man who laid it out named it after a friend.

William Mendenhall founded the town that year, after the Central Pacific railroad reached the valley, and named it for Robert Livermore. Livermore and Jose Noriega had secured Rancho Las Positas in 1839, and the city sits partly on that grant. Before Mendenhall's town there was Laddsville, the valley's first settlement. It grew around a hotel Alphonso Ladd opened in the 1860s. Sources give 1864 for the hotel in one place and the 1860s more loosely in another. The city incorporated on April 1, 1876.

Then wine. In the 1880s Wente, Concannon and Wetmore were doing work here that shaped the California wine industry. The Livermore Valley has been a wine region continuously since.

Downtown is the railroad town's grid, and it is the oldest ground in the city.

Livermore has 31,936 housing units and 4.5 percent of them predate 1950. 69.2 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 72.0 percent, and on both measures Livermore is second only to Piedmont among Alameda County cities, the ACS median value is 1,105,600 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,677. Downtown holds most of that pre war stock and what multi unit housing the city has.

So pull the year built, because this is the one part of Livermore where genuinely old housing is likely.

On pre war buildings: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the permit history on every addition. Ask whether the property carries any local historic designation before planning an exterior change.

Confirm the legal unit count with the city on anything that might hold more than one household.

Then the heat. Livermore sits inland and runs hotter than the rest of this series, so ask the age and condition of the cooling system specifically and what it costs to run through a summer. That is a real line item here in a way it is not in Alameda or Berkeley.

Then do a Saturday downtown on foot from the address.

What the market is doing right now

$1,071,869 is the typical Downtown Livermore home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.03 percent, and over the year down 2.3 percent.

Listing activity in Livermore for 2026-09. Active inventory is 159. 80 new listings came on, and 57 went pending. Median days on market is 33.

Median asking price is $1,061,695 at $649 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,071,869, up 0.03 percent month over month, down 2.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $10,160, or $121,923 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Livermore I cover, and what each one is:

  • Dunsmuir. Dunsmuir is one of Livermore's residential pockets with little published history of its own.
  • Granada. Granada is a postwar Livermore neighborhood whose record is the city's, not its own.
  • Mendenhall. This neighborhood is named for the man who founded the city.
  • North Livermore. North Livermore is the ground north of the old railroad grid, and its record is the city's.
  • Portola. Portola takes its name from the avenue it sits along, on the older northern side of Livermore.
  • South Livermore. South Livermore is the wine side of the city, and the wine goes back to the 1880s.
  • Springtown. Springtown sits on the northeastern side of Livermore and is one of the city's distinct postwar developments.
  • Sunset. Sunset is one of Livermore's established postwar neighborhoods and its published history belongs to the city.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $10,160 a month, $121,923 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. Alameda County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Downtown Livermore charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,071,869 home owes roughly $1,179 at transfer. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $590 each, though the contract decides.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Dublin charges 1.10 per thousand against Oakland at 16.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $16,078.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near -$56,651. At five years it reaches -$165,189.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

The full report

Everything behind these numbers lives in the full Downtown Livermore, Livermore report: the tables, the rate and loan detail, the tax math, holding costs, buyer programs, ADU rules and a dated source for each figure. item.content:encoded:
A man lost this whole valley at the card table, more or less, and it carries his name anyway.

Guillermo Castro received Rancho San Lorenzo from Governor Juan Alvarado. It covered what is now Hayward, San Lorenzo and Castro Valley, taking in Crow Canyon, Cull Canyon and Palomares Canyon. Castro gambled. Mayhew, presided over the sale of the last of it for 400,000 dollars to Faxon Atherton.

What survived is the name. Castro Valley is the largest community in unincorporated Alameda County. That is the other fact governing everything here: there is no city hall. The county runs the planning, the permits and most of the services, and that is the first thing a buyer should establish instead of assume.

Downtown runs along Castro Valley Boulevard with the Castro Valley BART station on it.

Then pull the year built and confirm the legal unit count with the county, not the listing.

On pre war stock: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the permit history on every addition.

Then the fault. The Hayward Fault runs along the western edge of this valley. Ask the title company whether the parcel sits inside an Alquist-Priolo earthquake fault zone and ask whether the house has ever been bolted to its foundation.

Then walk to the BART platform from the address and time it. In a valley where almost everything else is a drive, that walk is the premium.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Downtown Castro Valley home at $1,088,972 on 2026-09-30, up 0.16 percent month over month and up 1.2 percent year over year.

Listing activity in Castro Valley for 2026-09. Active inventory is 56. 34 new listings came on, and 25 went pending. Median days on market is 30.

Median asking price is $1,234,000 at $614 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,088,972, up 0.16 percent month over month, up 1.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $10,309, or $123,708 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.

Inside it

  • Lake Chabot Area. The Lake Chabot area is the northern edge of Castro Valley, up against the reservoir and the regional parkland around it.
  • Palomares Hills. Palomares Hills sits above the valley in one of the canyons that was part of Guillermo Castro's rancho, and the canyon still carries the Palomares name.
  • Parsons. Parsons is a Castro Valley neighborhood named for the avenue running through it.
  • Proctor. Proctor is one of Castro Valley's established residential neighborhoods, named for the school at its centre.

Put the minimum down on the typical Downtown Castro Valley home and the monthly carry lands near $10,309. That is $123,708 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Alameda County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

Downtown Castro Valley charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,088,972 home owes roughly $1,198 at transfer. Convention puts about $599 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

item.content:encoded:
Parsons is a Castro Valley neighborhood named for the avenue running through it.

Guillermo Castro received Rancho San Lorenzo from Governor Juan Alvarado. Most sources date the grant to 1841 and one book on the valley says 1843, and the size is given as either 26,722 acres or about 28,000. It covered what is now Hayward, San Lorenzo and Castro Valley, taking in Crow Canyon, Cull Canyon and Palomares Canyon. Castro gambled. He sold off pieces of the rancho to cover his debts, mortgaged what was left, and fought lawsuits from Gold Rush settlers trying to clear squatters. In 1864 the sheriff, I. A. Mayhew, presided over the sale of the last of it for 400,000 dollars to Faxon Atherton.

The practical consequence of all that today is simpler. Castro Valley is the largest community in unincorporated Alameda County, so there is no city hall. The county handles planning, permits and most services.

Castro Valley has 22,957 housing units and 16.9 percent of them predate 1950. 73.3 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 72.5 percent, both high for this series. The ACS median value is 1,104,600 dollars and the median gross rent is 2,554.

The stock here is consistent in era, and that is useful: where houses went up inside a narrow window, comparable sales genuinely compare and the whole price spread is condition and updates. Pull the year built, compare within the cohort, then put your effort into the inspection report.

The list for this era: the roof and its age, the supply lines, the electrical panel capacity if you intend to add load, the sewer lateral, the furnace and the water heater.

So confirm jurisdiction before anything else. Alameda County, not a city, issues your permits and sets your zoning, and you should ask what services actually come with the address.

Then the fault. The Hayward Fault runs along the western edge of this valley, so ask the title company whether the parcel sits inside an Alquist-Priolo earthquake fault zone and ask whether the house has ever been bolted to its foundation.

Then drive the route to the freeway or to BART at your real commute hour.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Parsons is $1,088,972: up 0.16 percent against last month, up 1.2 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Castro Valley for 2026-09. Active inventory is 56. 34 new listings came on, and 25 went pending. Median days on market is 30.

Median asking price is $1,234,000 at $614 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,088,972, up 0.16 percent month over month, up 1.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $10,309, or $123,708 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Alameda County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.42 percent (Alameda County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Castro Valley I cover, and what each one is:

  • Downtown Castro Valley. A man lost this whole valley at the card table, more or less, and it carries his name anyway.
  • Five Canyons. Five Canyons is a later planned development on the hill ground at the eastern edge of Castro Valley.
  • Jensen Ranch. Jensen Ranch is hillside development on the ridge above Castro Valley, built late and built large.
  • Lake Chabot Area. The Lake Chabot area is the northern edge of Castro Valley, up against the reservoir and the regional parkland around it.
  • Palomares Hills. Palomares Hills sits above the valley in one of the canyons that was part of Guillermo Castro's rancho, and the canyon still carries the Palomares name.
  • Proctor. Proctor is one of Castro Valley's established residential neighborhoods, named for the school at its centre.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $10,309 a month, $123,708 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Alameda County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

Parsons charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $1,088,972 home owes roughly $1,198 at transfer. Convention puts about $599 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $31,504. Stretch it to five and the figure is $96,873.

item.content:encoded:
Fairview is the unincorporated hill ground above Hayward, and the name describes what you get.

This ground was part of Guillermo Castro's Rancho San Lorenzo, granted by Governor Juan Alvarado and covering what is now Hayward, San Lorenzo and Castro Valley. Castro sold pieces of it to cover gambling debts, mortgaged the rest, and in 1864 the sheriff sold the last of it for 400,000 dollars to Faxon Atherton. The whole area was Eden Township, the agricultural district that supplied this side of the bay, and the Eden name still turns up on neighborhoods and schools around here. Fairview is the upper, sloping part of that ground, running up toward Garin Regional Park and the ridge.

Being unincorporated on a hillside means two sets of questions stack on each other.

So jurisdiction is the first thing to establish, and it is not a formality.

This is unincorporated Alameda County. There is no city hall. The county issues the permits, sets the zoning and provides most of the services, so get your answers there, and ask specifically what refuse, sewer, water and road maintenance arrangements come with the address. Buyers routinely assume city services on unincorporated ground and are wrong.

Then the fault. The Hayward Fault runs along the hills immediately east of here. Ask the title company whether the parcel sits inside an Alquist-Priolo earthquake fault zone and ask whether the house has ever been bolted to its foundation.

Then the house, matched to its year built. On pre war stock: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines and the permit history on every addition. On postwar stock: the roof, the supply lines, the electrical panel capacity, the sewer lateral, the furnace and the water heater.

Confirm the legal unit count with the county, not the listing, because conversions happen here and the permits often do not.

Then check the lot dimensions and setbacks if an accessory dwelling unit is part of your plan.

Then the hillside list. It applies to most of this community. Ask for the soils and drainage history on the parcel. Ask who owns and maintains any retaining structures and in what condition, because a failing retaining wall is the most expensive surprise on a hill lot and it is frequently a shared obligation. Ask the inspector where water leaves the property in a wet month.

Then get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address before your contingencies expire, with the risk rating explained, because this is hill ground against regional parkland and carriers price it accordingly.

item.content:encoded:
Sunol has 330 housing units in total. That is the whole place.

It sits in the hills between Fremont and Pleasanton, unincorporated, in a valley the water system runs through. 97.3 percent of its housing is single family detached, among the highest shares anywhere in this series, and 43.6 percent of it predates 1950. Owner occupancy runs 82.1 percent. The ACS median value is 1,333,300 dollars.

One thing does run through Sunol, and it is a railway. The Niles Canyon Railway operates on the original alignment of the First Transcontinental Railroad, the eleven mile section between Sunol and the Niles district of Fremont. The National Register listed that stretch on October 13, 2010 as the Niles Canyon Transcontinental Railroad Historic District. The Pacific Locomotive Association leased the right of way and began rebuilding track in 1987, and the first passenger train ran out of Sunol on May 21, 1988. Trains still run it.

So the valley that holds 330 homes also holds the western end of the line that first connected California to the rest of the country, and the depot is a short walk from most of the housing.

A town of three hundred and thirty homes does not behave like a market. In a normal month there may be no sales at all. The usual tools stop working: there is often nothing to compare a house against, and an index built on thin transaction volume moves on very little. Anyone pricing a Sunol property should expect to reason from the land and the condition instead of from recent comparable sales, and should treat any automated valuation with real caution.

So the work here is different from anywhere else in this series.

Establish jurisdiction. Sunol is unincorporated, so Alameda County handles planning and permits and you should ask exactly which services come with the address.

Ask about water and waste. On parcels this size, ask whether the property is on a well or on district water, and if a well, for the yield and the water quality testing. Ask about any septic system, when it was last inspected and when it was last pumped.

Ask about access. Ask whether the road to the property is public or private, and if private, who maintains it and under what agreement, because that is a recorded obligation that transfers with the land.

Then the house, matched to its year built, with foundation bolting on anything pre war.

And get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address early, with the risk rating explained. In a small valley surrounded by open hills that quote can be the deciding number.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

A railroad picked this spot and the city grew around it afterward.

The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe put its western terminus at Point Richmond, in 1899 by one account and on July 4, 1900 by another, with ferries running across to San Francisco. The settlement around the terminal was called East Yards first. The name Point Richmond came later. From the late 1800s into the early 1900s this was Richmond's downtown.

Standard Oil built its refinery here in 1901, with one account giving 1902. By 1904 it was reported as the second largest oil refinery in the world. Chevron runs it today. The city incorporated in 1905, after the refinery, not before it.

Point Richmond kept its street pattern and a good deal of its building stock while the city expanded east around the refinery and the shipyards. The result is a small pre war commercial village with a tunnel at one end and the refinery on the hill above it.

Richmond has 42,509 housing units and 28.5 percent of them predate 1950. 59.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 54.7 percent, and the ACS median value is 668,200 dollars. In Point Richmond the pre war share runs well above that 28.5 percent.

Pull the year built. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history. Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

On pre war stock: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of original windows and siding.

Ask for the site history in writing on any parcel with an industrial past. Richmond has a century of heavy industry in it and the record is public.

And ask about the refinery specifically. Ask your insurance broker how the proximity is rated and ask the city what notification and emergency systems cover the address. Those are answerable questions and a buyer here should have the answers in hand.

Then walk the village end to end. It takes about fifteen minutes and it is the clearest surviving piece of what Richmond looked like before the war.

  • Brickyard Cove. Brickyard Cove is named for what used to be here, and the shoreline is the whole reason to buy.
  • Carriage Hills. Carriage Hills is hill ground on Richmond's eastern edge.
  • Clinton Hill. Clinton Hill is on the rising eastern side of Richmond.
  • Coronado. Coronado is one of Richmond's older flatland neighborhoods, south of the city centre.
  • Cortez Stege. Cortez and Stege are the two names on this neighborhood at the southern end of Richmond.
  • East Richmond Heights. East Richmond Heights sits on the slope above the city, and part of it is unincorporated county ground.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $8,472 a month to own the typical home in Point Richmond, $101,663 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. In Contra Costa County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 8.10 dollars per thousand, a $887,118 sale in Point Richmond carries about $7,186 in transfer tax. Expect it split, near enough $3,593 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $1,000,000 the rate steps from 8.10 to 13.50 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,400 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $1,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

item.content:encoded:
Atchison Village was built to house the people building ships.

Henry Kaiser opened his first Richmond shipyard in December 1940. The city had fewer than 24,000 people that year and nearly 100,000 by 1943. Four yards here built 747 ships, more than any other shipyard complex in the country. The Rosie the Riveter World War II Home Front National Historical Park was dedicated on October 25, 2000 and was the first national park created to commemorate the home front. Atchison Village is one of the worker housing projects from that period and it is part of the story the national park tells. The name comes from the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroad. It put its western terminus at Point Richmond around the turn of the century and gave this ground its first industry.

What makes it unusual today is that it survived. Most wartime housing in the Bay Area was temporary by design and was cleared afterward. This was not.

Richmond has 42,509 housing units and 28.5 percent of them predate 1950. 59.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 54.7 percent, and the ACS median value is 668,200 dollars. Atchison Village sits at the older end of that range.

So the first thing to establish on any address here is the ownership structure, because it is not an ordinary subdivision. Ask the title company exactly what you would be buying, how the community is organised, what the governing documents say, and what the transfer process requires. Get that in writing before anything else, because it determines whether a conventional loan is even available.

Then the housing itself. This is wartime construction and it is eighty years old now. Ask about the foundation and whether it has ever been bolted. Ask about the supply lines, the electrical panel and its capacity, the roof, and the windows.

Ask for the site history in writing, since this ground sits inside a century old industrial district.

Then go look at the Rosie the Riveter visitor centre before you decide. The park explains what these houses were for, and that context is most of what makes the neighborhood what it is.

What the market is doing right now

Atchison Village sits at $200,104 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.11 percent since last month and down 1.6 percent since last year.

Listing activity in Richmond for 2026-09. Active inventory is 115. 54 new listings came on, and 66 went pending. Median days on market is 30.

Median asking price is $560,113 at $509 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $200,104, up 0.11 percent month over month, down 1.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $2,559, or $30,710 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Richmond I cover, and what each one is:

  • Belding Woods. Belding and Woods are the two names this central Richmond neighborhood carries.
  • Brickyard Cove. Brickyard Cove is named for what used to be here, and the shoreline is the whole reason to buy.
  • Carriage Hills. Carriage Hills is hill ground on Richmond's eastern edge.
  • Clinton Hill. Clinton Hill is on the rising eastern side of Richmond.
  • Coronado. Coronado is one of Richmond's older flatland neighborhoods, south of the city centre.
  • Cortez Stege. Cortez and Stege are the two names on this neighborhood at the southern end of Richmond.
  • East Richmond Heights. East Richmond Heights sits on the slope above the city, and part of it is unincorporated county ground.
  • Fairmede Hilltop. Fairmede and Hilltop are the two names on this neighborhood in north Richmond, near the Hilltop commercial district.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $2,559 monthly, or $30,710 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

Transfer tax on the typical Atchison Village home, $200,104, comes to roughly $1,621 at a rate of 8.10 per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $810 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

At $1,000,000 the rate steps from 8.10 to 13.50 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,400 more than a sale one dollar under it. item.title: Parchester Village, Richmond: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Parchester Village, Richmond housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $472,024, down 0.05 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Parchester Village is a planned postwar community at the northern edge of Richmond, laid out as a single development with its own street pattern and its own community organisation.

Standard Oil built its refinery here in 1901, with one account giving 1902. By 1904 it was reported as the second largest oil refinery in the world. Chevron runs it today. The city incorporated in 1905, after the refinery, not before it.

Henry Kaiser opened his first Richmond shipyard in December 1940. The city had fewer than 24,000 people that year and nearly 100,000 by 1943. Four yards here built 747 ships, more than any other shipyard complex in the country. The Rosie the Riveter World War II Home Front National Historical Park was dedicated on October 25, 2000 and was the first national park created to commemorate the home front.

Richmond has 42,509 housing units and 28.5 percent of them predate 1950. 59.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 54.7 percent, and the ACS median value is 668,200 dollars.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history. Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

On pre war stock: foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of original windows and siding.

Ask for the site history in writing on any parcel with an industrial past. Richmond has a century of heavy industry in it and the record is public.

Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it. Richmond has heavy industry woven through its flats and a permitted use next door is not always what operates there now.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Parchester Village is $472,024: down 0.05 percent against last month, down 3.6 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Richmond for 2026-09. Active inventory is 115. 54 new listings came on, and 66 went pending. Median days on market is 30.

Median asking price is $560,113 at $509 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $472,024, down 0.05 percent month over month, down 3.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $4,899, or $58,794 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Richmond I cover, and what each one is:

  • Atchison Village. Atchison Village was built to house the people building ships.
  • Belding Woods. Belding and Woods are the two names this central Richmond neighborhood carries.
  • Brickyard Cove. Brickyard Cove is named for what used to be here, and the shoreline is the whole reason to buy.
  • Carriage Hills. Carriage Hills is hill ground on Richmond's eastern edge.
  • Clinton Hill. Clinton Hill is on the rising eastern side of Richmond.
  • Coronado. Coronado is one of Richmond's older flatland neighborhoods, south of the city centre.
  • Cortez Stege. Cortez and Stege are the two names on this neighborhood at the southern end of Richmond.
  • East Richmond Heights. East Richmond Heights sits on the slope above the city, and part of it is unincorporated county ground.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $4,899 a month, $58,794 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. Contra Costa County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Parchester Village charges 8.10 per thousand, so the typical $472,024 home owes roughly $3,823 at transfer. It is normally split down the middle, about $1,912 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

The part that costs people money is the bracket. The rate that applies is charged on the ENTIRE sale price, not only the amount above the line. At $1,000,000 the rate steps from 8.10 to 13.50 per thousand, so a sale one dollar over that line pays about $5,400 more than a sale one dollar under it. On anything pricing near $1,000,000, the number to run is not the percentage. It is which side of the line the contract price lands on.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $5,664.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near -$38,335. At five years it reaches -$109,702.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

El Cerrito was built by refugees and it was called Rust first. People leaving San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake settled on what was then Don Victor Castro's Rancho San Pablo. The post office opened in 1909 with Rust as the first postmaster on March 1 of that year. The residents disliked the name and changed it to El Cerrito, Little Hill. The village incorporated on August 23, 1917 with about 1,500 people, on a vote of 158 to 131.

The Cerrito Theatre at 10070 San Pablo Avenue opened in 1937 in Art Deco, closed in 1966, and was restored forty years later by the El Cerrito Redevelopment Agency. Victor Castro's adobe stood in the El Cerrito Plaza area until it burned in 1956.

item.content:encoded:
Victoria by the Bay is a planned shoreline development in Hercules.

Hercules is named after dynamite. The California Powder Works developed this site in 1881 to make its patented explosive, Hercules powder, and the town took the product's name. The company's managers incorporated the town itself on December 15, 1900, because they could not get the county supervisors to pass the laws they wanted for the plant. The corporate history is tangled: an earlier Hercules Powder Company was incorporated in 1882 by DuPont with Laflin and Rand and DuPont dissolved it in 1904, and a later one was incorporated on October 18, 1912 and began business in January 1913.

Hercules has 9,581 housing units and 0.5 percent of them predate 1950. For a town incorporated in 1900 that is the whole modern history of the place in one number: almost everything standing here went up long after the powder works. 57.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 79.2 percent, and the ACS median value is 769,400 dollars. ZHVI is about 736,000 dollars, down 0.7 percent over the year.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and the year each one expires, in writing. A newly built East County subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about grading and drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Get the flood zone determination for the parcel with a written insurance quote, and ask the inspector about settlement and about the condition and ownership of any bulkhead, levee or revetment the property sits behind. On the water that is the most expensive thing that can go wrong and it is frequently shared.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

item.content:encoded:
Baywood is a residential subdivision in Hercules.

Hercules is named after dynamite. The California Powder Works developed this site in 1881 to make its patented explosive, Hercules powder, and the town took the product's name. The company's managers incorporated the town itself on December 15, 1900, because they could not get the county supervisors to pass the laws they wanted for the plant. The corporate history is tangled: an earlier Hercules Powder Company was incorporated in 1882 by DuPont with Laflin and Rand and DuPont dissolved it in 1904, and a later one was incorporated on October 18, 1912 and began business in January 1913.

Hercules has 9,581 housing units and 0.5 percent of them predate 1950. For a town incorporated in 1900 that is the whole modern history of the place in one number: almost everything standing here went up long after the powder works. 57.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 79.2 percent, and the ACS median value is 769,400 dollars. ZHVI is about 736,000 dollars, down 0.7 percent over the year.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and the year each one expires, in writing. A newly built East County subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about grading and drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Baywood is $735,539: up 0.41 percent against last month, down 0.7 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Hercules for 2026-09. Active inventory is 36. 14 new listings came on, and 15 went pending. Median days on market is 39.

Inside it

  • Bayside. Bayside is on the shoreline side of Hercules.
  • Hercules Historic District. The Hercules Historic District is what survives of the powder works town.
  • Refugio Valley. Refugio Valley runs inland in Hercules, and the park and the road carry the name.
  • Victoria By The Bay. Victoria by the Bay is a planned shoreline development in Hercules.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $7,167 monthly, or $86,009 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. Contra Costa County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Baywood charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $735,539 home owes roughly $809 at transfer. Convention puts about $405 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $8,826.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$11,121 here. The five year figure is -$33,238.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

item.content:encoded:
Downtown Lafayette runs along Mt. Diablo Boulevard, and the line of that street was set by a grist mill.

Lafayette started as a Mexican land grant. Rancho Acalanes was granted in 1834 to Candelario Valencia, and Elam Brown was its third owner. Brown's party reached the area in 1846 and settled in 1848. Accounts of the purchase differ, one putting it at 1847 for 900 dollars across 3,328.9 acres and another at 1848. Brown built a horse powered grist mill in 1849 and the commerce that gathered around it set the line of what is now Mt. Diablo Boulevard. Brown served as alcalde, sat in the state constitutional convention of 1849, and served in California's first two legislatures. The city itself did not incorporate until 1968.

Lafayette has 9,998 housing units and 16.5 percent of them predate 1950, a high pre war share for this part of the county. 74.3 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 77.1 percent. ZHVI is about 1,907,000 dollars, up 3.5 percent over the year. One number to read carefully. The ACS reports a median owner occupied value of 2,000,001 dollars here, and that is the survey's ceiling, not a measurement. The actual median sits above the highest figure the survey will print.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Get the permit history for the parcel.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Elam Brown's horse powered mill of 1849 drew the commerce that became this street. Downtown adds two questions. Pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours, because these blocks mix retail, office and residential. And ask the city whether the address sits inside a downtown specific plan area, since that governs what can be built across the street from you.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

  • Burton Valley. Burton Valley is the southern side of Lafayette, in the hills below the ridge.
  • Happy Valley. Happy Valley is the north side of Lafayette, up the valley from the old town centre.
  • Lafayette Moraga Corridor. This is the ground along the route between Lafayette and Moraga, and the regional trail that runs it is the spine of the corridor.
  • Reliez Valley. Reliez Valley runs between Lafayette and Pleasant Hill, and part of it is unincorporated.
  • Springhill. Springhill is the northern end of Lafayette, on the rising ground toward the Briones hills.
  • Upper Happy Valley. Upper Happy Valley is the higher ground at the top of the same valley, and the altitude changes the questions.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $17,252 a month to own the typical home in Downtown Lafayette, $207,026 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

At 1.10 dollars per thousand, a $1,907,310 sale in Downtown Lafayette carries about $2,098 in transfer tax. It is normally split down the middle, about $1,049 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $23,651.

item.title: Orinda Country Club area, Orinda: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Orinda Country Club area, Orinda housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $1,942,797, up 0.59 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
The Orinda Country Club area is the neighborhood around the club on the north side of the city.

Orinda was a weekend place before a tunnel made it a town. The Caldecott Tunnel opened in 1937 and is credited with turning the area into a year round community. The Orinda Theatre opened in December 1941, and its dorsal fin marquee is still the most recognisable object in the city. Sources give the opening as December 27 and as December 17, so the exact day is contested. Orinda did not become a city until July 1, 1985, the eighteenth in Contra Costa County, on a March 5 vote of 4,687 to 3,293. Orinda also holds the county's oldest surviving adobe. The Moraga Adobe was built in 1841 by Joaquin Moraga and it is the oldest of the five surviving adobe houses in Contra Costa County. The name misleads people: it stands on Adobe Lane in Orinda, not in the town of Moraga. The land grant behind it is dated 1835.

Orinda has 7,475 housing units and 17.9 percent of them predate 1950, the highest pre war share in Lamorinda. 94.6 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 91.3 percent. The ACS median value is 1,863,200 dollars and ZHVI is about 1,943,000, up 2.6 percent over the year.

So the buying questions out here are hill questions and they come before the house.

Ask the inspector about soils and drainage on the parcel and about where water leaves it in a wet month. Ask about the condition and the ownership of every retaining structure, because a shared retaining wall on a slope is the most expensive thing that can go wrong.

Get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address with the risk rating explained, and ask what the insurer wants cleared to write it. In this part of the county that quote decides deals.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Club membership and home ownership are two separate things and they are frequently confused here. Ask in writing whether any membership transfers with the property, what the initiation and dues are, and whether there is a waiting list. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Orinda Country Club area sits at $1,942,797 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.59 percent since last month and up 2.6 percent since last year.

Listing activity in Orinda for 2026-09. Active inventory is 33. 26 new listings came on, and 20 went pending. Median days on market is 23.

Median asking price is $1,921,250 at $738 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,942,797, up 0.59 percent month over month, up 2.6 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $17,558, or $210,691 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Orinda I cover, and what each one is:

  • Del Rey. Del Rey is a residential neighborhood in Orinda, near the school of the same name.
  • Downtown Orinda. Downtown Orinda is small, and the theatre is the landmark.
  • Glorietta. Glorietta is a residential neighborhood on the southern side of Orinda.
  • Ridgewood. Ridgewood sits on the higher ground in Orinda, and the name is accurate.
  • Sleepy Hollow. Sleepy Hollow is on the northern side of Orinda, in the hills.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $17,558 a month to own the typical home in Orinda Country Club area, $210,691 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,942,797 here, transfer tax runs about $2,137 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $1,069 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $24,091.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $117,318, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $368,033.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

Saint Mary's College moved here in 1928 and the campus has shaped the town ever since. The town is young as a jurisdiction. An incorporation election carried in November 1974, with November 13 given as the date, and the town was assembled out of three places that had grown separately: Moraga Town, Rheem and Rheem Valley.   • Monthly cost of owning it: $14,666, or $175,990 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Moraga I cover, and what each one is:

  • Campolindo. Campolindo is a Moraga neighborhood on the hill ground, and it shares its name with the high school.
  • Moraga Country Club. Moraga Country Club is a gated community built around a golf course.
  • Rheem Valley. Rheem Valley is the eastern side of Moraga, around the Rheem commercial centre.
  • Sanders Ranch. Sanders Ranch is a subdivision on the eastern edge of Moraga, out where the town meets open ground.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $14,666 a month, $175,990 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,606,792 here, transfer tax runs about $1,767 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Convention puts about $884 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $19,924.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $125,405. Stretch it to five and the figure is $397,806.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

The first inhabitants of this valley were the Saklan people, of the Bay Miwok group, though one account names the Ohlone instead. One correction worth carrying: the Moraga Adobe that Joaquin Moraga built in 1841 stands on Adobe Lane in Orinda, not in this town.

Moraga has 5,719 housing units and only 1.6 percent of them predate 1950. 66.8 percent are single family detached, a lower detached share than its Lamorinda neighbours, and owner occupancy runs 83.1 percent. The ACS median value is 1,663,200 dollars and ZHVI is about 1,607,000, up 3.3 percent over the year.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and when each one expires, in writing. A newly built valley subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about the grading and the drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Three things come before the house. Get the governing documents and read what the association controls, since a gated community governs more than a standard subdivision does. Ask in writing whether club membership transfers with the property and what it costs. And ask your lender early whether it will finance in this community.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Moraga Country Club sits at $1,606,792 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.59 percent since last month and up 3.3 percent since last year.

Listing activity in Moraga for 2026-09. Active inventory is 31. 24 new listings came on, and 12 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $937,250 at $614 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,606,792, up 0.59 percent month over month, up 3.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $14,666, or $175,990 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Moraga I cover, and what each one is:

  • Campolindo. Campolindo is a Moraga neighborhood on the hill ground, and it shares its name with the high school.
  • Central Moraga. Central Moraga is the town centre, and Saint Mary's College has shaped it since 1928.
  • Rheem Valley. Rheem Valley is the eastern side of Moraga, around the Rheem commercial centre.
  • Sanders Ranch. Sanders Ranch is a subdivision on the eastern edge of Moraga, out where the town meets open ground.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $14,666 a month to own the typical home in Moraga Country Club, $175,990 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Moraga Country Club home, $1,606,792, comes to roughly $1,767 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $884 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $19,924.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $125,405, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $397,806.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

item.content:encoded:
Concord's town square is older than the city's name.

Concord started as a Mexican land grant. Rancho Monte del Diablo went to Salvio Pacheco in 1834. In 1868 the Pacheco family and Francisco Galindo laid out a town on it called Todos Santos, and the Contra Costa Gazette announced the new name Concord on April 17, 1869. The plaza at the centre of it covers 2.5 acres, bounded by Salvio Street, Willow Pass Road, Grant Street and Mount Diablo Street. Sources put its dedication at 1868 and at 1869, so the exact year is contested. In 2018 the American Planning Association named it one of three Great Places in California.

A detail most buyers never hear: a number of the historic houses standing around the plaza were not built where they sit. They were moved here from other parts of Concord to keep them from being demolished.

The farmers market runs on Tuesdays year round, with a second market on Thursday evenings in the warm months. Published hours conflict across three sources, so check the city's current schedule and do not trust a listing on it.

Concord has 47,703 housing units and 6.7 percent of them predate 1950. 58.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 61.6 percent, and the ACS median value is 797,600 dollars. The city's own figure is that 73 percent of its existing homes went up between 1950 and 1979. Around the plaza the pre war share runs above that citywide 6.7 percent.

So the buying questions in Concord are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a 1950s or 1960s tract house, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

Original aluminium windows and an original kitchen are either the discount or the asset here. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in.

Downtown adds two more. Pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours, because the blocks off the plaza mix commercial and residential and what is permitted next door is not always what operates there now. And ask the city whether the address falls in any downtown specific plan area, since that governs what can be built across the street from you.

One thing hangs over every address in this city. The former Concord Naval Weapons Station covers roughly 2,225 acres and the reuse plan calls for more than 12,000 homes, 6 million square feet of commercial space and more than 800 acres of parks, with Brookfield Properties as master developer. The city announced on September 24, 2026 that the Navy had approved the term sheet, and the governor signed SB 328, exempting the project from the Surplus Land Act and streamlining its environmental review. The site is a federal Superfund site with lead and arsenic in it and the Navy has to finish the cleanup before anything gets built. Nobody can tell you the delivery date.

And ask your agent to put the base reuse timeline in writing as a range, not a date. A buyer three miles from 12,000 future homes is making a bet on traffic, schools and supply, and nobody honest will give you a single year for it.

Then stand in the plaza on a Tuesday and again on a Sunday. It is the same two and a half acres and it is a different place.

What the market is doing right now

Todos Santos sits at $720,907 in typical value as of 2026-09-30, having moved up 0.37 percent since last month and up 0.2 percent since last year.

Listing activity in Concord for 2026-09. Active inventory is 203. 86 new listings came on, and 70 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $751,719 at $467 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $720,907, up 0.37 percent month over month, up 0.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,041, or $84,498 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Concord I cover, and what each one is:

  • Cambridge. Cambridge is a central Concord neighborhood, and Cambridge Park is the open space the city names inside it.
  • Clayton Valley. Clayton Valley is the eastern side of Concord, running toward the city of Clayton and the foot of Mount Diablo.
  • Colony Park. Colony Park is a postwar residential neighborhood in Concord.
  • Dana Estates. Dana Estates is one of Concord's postwar residential tracts.
  • Holbrook Heights. Holbrook Heights is on the rising ground on Concord's northern side.
  • Limeridge. Lime Ridge is named for a quarry operation.
  • Monument Corridor. This neighborhood is named for a street.
  • Northgate. Northgate sits on Concord's southern edge, on the Walnut Creek side of the city, below the Mount Diablo foothills.

What it costs to own here

Owning that typical home runs about $7,041 a month, $84,498 a year, once the loan, the property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget are all counted. HOA dues are not in it, because they vary by building.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. Contra Costa County's 2026 one-unit loan limit sits at $1,249,125. That is the cap for conforming conventional and for FHA alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $720,907 here, transfer tax runs about $793 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $396 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $8,651.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $3,028. Stretch it to five and the figure is $9,163.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

item.title: Ygnacio Valley, Concord: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Ygnacio Valley, Concord housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $720,907, up 0.37 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Ygnacio Valley Road runs the length of this part of Concord and the neighborhood takes its name from the valley.

Ygnacio Valley Park sits at the northeast corner of Oak Grove Road and David Avenue. The city lists it at 9.5 acres, with trails, picnic tables and sports fields. Newhall Community Park is the larger one nearby, 126.1 acres by the city's count, running along Galindo Creek east of Treat Boulevard, with roughly 30 acres of it improved with ponds, a play structure, picnic areas, bocce courts and athletic fields.

Concord started as a Mexican land grant. Rancho Monte del Diablo went to Salvio Pacheco in 1834. In 1868 the Pacheco family and Francisco Galindo laid out a town on it called Todos Santos, and the Contra Costa Gazette announced the new name Concord on April 17, 1869.

The city filled in after that on a tight schedule. Park and Shop and then Sun Valley Mall opened as regional shopping destinations through the 1950s and 1960s, and BART reached Concord in 1973. Joseph Eichler built three tracts here, Rancho Del Diablo, Rancho Los Santos and Parkwood Estates, roughly 175 homes in 1963 and 1964.

Concord has 47,703 housing units and 6.7 percent of them predate 1950. 58.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 61.6 percent, and the ACS median value is 797,600 dollars. The city's own figure is that 73 percent of its existing homes went up between 1950 and 1979. This side of Concord is squarely inside that 1950 to 1979 band.

So the buying questions in Concord are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a 1950s or 1960s tract house, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

Original aluminium windows and an original kitchen are either the discount or the asset here. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in.

Add the creek. Galindo Creek runs through this area, so get the flood zone determination for the parcel with a written insurance quote, and ask the inspector about drainage and about where water leaves the property in a wet month.

One thing hangs over every address in this city. The former Concord Naval Weapons Station covers roughly 2,225 acres and the reuse plan calls for more than 12,000 homes, 6 million square feet of commercial space and more than 800 acres of parks, with Brookfield Properties as master developer. The city announced on September 24, 2026 that the Navy had approved the term sheet, and the governor signed SB 328, exempting the project from the Surplus Land Act and streamlining its environmental review. The site is a federal Superfund site with lead and arsenic in it and the Navy has to finish the cleanup before anything gets built. Nobody can tell you the delivery date.

And ask your agent to put the base reuse timeline in writing as a range, not a date. A buyer three miles from 12,000 future homes is making a bet on traffic, schools and supply, and nobody honest will give you a single year for it.

Then drive Ygnacio Valley Road at your real commute hour, and walk to the park from the address to see how long it actually takes.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Ygnacio Valley is $720,907 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.37 percent from the month before and up 0.2 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Concord for 2026-09. Active inventory is 203. 86 new listings came on, and 70 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $751,719 at $467 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $720,907, up 0.37 percent month over month, up 0.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,041, or $84,498 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Concord I cover, and what each one is:

  • Cambridge. Cambridge is a central Concord neighborhood, and Cambridge Park is the open space the city names inside it.
  • Clayton Valley. Clayton Valley is the eastern side of Concord, running toward the city of Clayton and the foot of Mount Diablo.
  • Colony Park. Colony Park is a postwar residential neighborhood in Concord.
  • Dana Estates. Dana Estates is one of Concord's postwar residential tracts.
  • Holbrook Heights. Holbrook Heights is on the rising ground on Concord's northern side.
  • Limeridge. Lime Ridge is named for a quarry operation.
  • Monument Corridor. This neighborhood is named for a street.
  • Northgate. Northgate sits on Concord's southern edge, on the Walnut Creek side of the city, below the Mount Diablo foothills.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $7,041 a month to own the typical home in Ygnacio Valley, $84,498 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Ygnacio Valley charges 1.10 per thousand, so the typical $720,907 home owes roughly $793 at transfer. Local practice splits it down the middle, roughly $396 each, though the contract decides.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $8,651.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near $3,028. At five years it reaches $9,163.

The input is a single trailing year, projected. It is not a forecast, and the five year number is the one to distrust first.

The full report

Everything behind these numbers lives in the full Ygnacio Valley, Concord report: the tables, the rate and loan detail, the tax math, holding costs, buyer programs, ADU rules and a dated source for each figure. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/concord/ygnacio-valley/.

item.content:encoded:
Downtown Walnut Creek is the commercial centre of central Contra Costa County, and the street at the middle of it is the reason the city incorporated.

Walnut Creek was called The Corners until the post office renamed it in 1862. The Southern Pacific arrived in 1891. It became the eighth city in Contra Costa County on October 21, 1914, by a vote of 127 to 67, with a population of about 500 and Harry Spencer as its first board president. One account says the voters wanted incorporation partly so the town could tax itself to pave Main Street. BART arrived in 1973.

Main Street is the thread here. One account of the 1914 incorporation vote has the taxing power to pave Main Street as a motive for it. The street now anchors a retail district that draws from the whole of central county.

Walnut Creek has 34,389 housing units and only 5.3 percent of them predate 1950. 36.8 percent are single family detached, the lowest detached share of any large city in this county. Owner occupancy runs 64.4 percent and the ACS median value is 1,057,300 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 990,000 dollars, up 1.3 percent over the year.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

item.content:encoded:
Saranap is not in Walnut Creek. It is unincorporated Contra Costa County territory between Walnut Creek and Lafayette, and that is the first thing to establish about any address here.

Walnut Creek was called The Corners until the post office renamed it in 1862. The Southern Pacific arrived in 1891. It became the eighth city in Contra Costa County on October 21, 1914, by a vote of 127 to 67, with a population of about 500 and Harry Spencer as its first board president. One account says the voters wanted incorporation partly so the town could tax itself to pave Main Street. BART arrived in 1973.

The area sits along the old interurban alignment between the two towns and filled in around it. Walnut Creek grew up on the other side of the line, from The Corners in 1862 to the county's eighth city on October 21, 1914 and a BART stop in 1973.

Walnut Creek has 34,389 housing units and only 5.3 percent of them predate 1950. 36.8 percent are single family detached, the lowest detached share of any large city in this county. Owner occupancy runs 64.4 percent and the ACS median value is 1,057,300 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 990,000 dollars, up 1.3 percent over the year.

So the buying questions are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

An original kitchen and original aluminium windows are either the discount or the asset. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in.

Then the part specific to this address. Confirm the address is unincorporated before anything else, because it changes who issues your permits, who provides your services, who polices it and what your tax bill looks like. Get it from the county, not from a listing. Then ask which school district serves the parcel, since district lines out here do not follow the lines a buyer expects. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. It carries the recording date, the original lot dimensions and the street layout as approved, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

Downtown Pleasant Hill is a built downtown, laid out long after the city's housing.

Pleasant Hill became a city to stop a neighbour. So the buying questions are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

An original kitchen and original aluminium windows are either the discount or the asset. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours, and ask the city whether the address sits inside a downtown specific plan area, since that governs what gets built across the street.

And pull the tax bill for the exact address off the county roll before you write anything, not the listing estimate. Read which districts and assessments appear on it and what each one charges. That document is free, it takes a day to get, and it is the difference between the payment a buyer expects and the payment they get.

  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.

  • Poets Corner. Poets Corner is a Pleasant Hill neighborhood where the streets carry poets' names.

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $9,211 monthly, or $110,537 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. In Contra Costa County the 2026 one-unit limit is $1,249,125. It serves as the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling at once.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

At 1.10 dollars per thousand, a $973,036 sale in Downtown carries about $1,070 in transfer tax. Convention puts about $535 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $11,676.

What waiting costs

Price and payment together, a two year wait here runs about $28,927. Stretch it to five and the figure is $88,993.

item.content:encoded:
Downtown Martinez is a county seat downtown, and it has been the county seat since 1850.

Martinez was laid out in 1849 by Col. William M. Smith and named for Ygnacio Martinez. It became the county seat in 1850 and it has been ever since. It could not incorporate at the time, because it did not have the 200 registered voters the law required, and it did not become a city until 1876. Rumours that the oil companies were coming set off a real estate rush in 1912, and Shell located here in 1915.

The John Muir National Historic Site is here. The house was built in 1883 by Dr. John Strentzel, Muir's father in law. Muir came to Martinez in 1880, lived in this house from 1890, and died in it in 1914. Martinez also claims the martini, from a local bartender's Martinez Special in 1849. San Francisco and several other cities claim it too, so the claim is disputed and should be told that way. Joe DiMaggio was born in this city.

Martinez has 15,178 housing units and 14.0 percent of them predate 1950, a high pre war share for this county, behind El Cerrito, Richmond and San Pablo. 63.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 70.8 percent, the highest of the six, and the ACS median value is 859,800 dollars. So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history.
