item.description: What the Alhambra Valley, Martinez housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $749,729, up 0.25 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Alhambra Valley is the oldest named ground in Martinez. It was inside the Rancho El Pinole grant made to Ygnacio Martinez in 1824.

Martinez was laid out in 1849 by Col. William M. Smith and named for Ygnacio Martinez. It became the county seat in 1850 and it has been ever since. It could not incorporate at the time, because it did not have the 200 registered voters the law required, and it did not become a city until 1876. Rumours that the oil companies were coming set off a real estate rush in 1912, and Shell located here in 1915.

The John Muir National Historic Site is here. The house was built in 1883 by Dr. John Strentzel, Muir's father in law. Muir came to Martinez in 1880, lived in this house from 1890, and died in it in 1914. The valley kept its rural character longer than the rest of the city and parts of it are still large lot.

Martinez has 15,178 housing units and 14.0 percent of them predate 1950, a high pre war share for this county, behind El Cerrito, Richmond and San Pablo. 63.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 70.8 percent, the highest of the six, and the ACS median value is 859,800 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 750,000 dollars, down 1.3 percent over the year.

So the buying questions are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

An original kitchen and original aluminium windows are either the discount or the asset. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in.

Then the part specific to this address. Out here, confirm three things. Whether the address is inside the city or in unincorporated county territory, because it changes your permits and your services. Whether the parcel is on a septic system or on sewer, and if septic, get the most recent inspection and the pumping record. And whether water comes from a district or a well, and if a well, get the yield and water quality tests in writing. On the higher ground, ask the inspector about soils and drainage on the parcel and about where water leaves it in a wet month. Ask about the condition and the ownership of any retaining structure, because a shared retaining wall on a slope is the most expensive thing that can go wrong here. Get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address with the risk rating explained.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Alhambra Valley is $749,729 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.25 percent from the month before and down 1.3 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Martinez for 2026-09. Active inventory is 78. 34 new listings came on, and 37 went pending. Median days on market is 38.

Median asking price is $783,250 at $490 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $749,729, up 0.25 percent month over month, down 1.3 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $7,290, or $87,474 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Martinez I cover, and what each one is:

  • Downtown Martinez. Downtown Martinez is a county seat downtown, and it has been the county seat since 1850.
  • Franklin Hills. Franklin Hills is hill ground on the Martinez side of the ridge.
  • Morello. Morello is a residential neighborhood in Martinez, along Morello Avenue on the city's eastern side.
  • Mountain View. Mountain View is a residential neighborhood in Martinez.
  • Virginia Hills. Virginia Hills sits on the rising ground in Martinez.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $7,290 a month to own the typical home in Alhambra Valley, $87,474 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $749,729 here, transfer tax runs about $825 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $412 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $8,997.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$22,344 here. The five year figure is -$66,145.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

Downtown Clayton is a small town centre at the foot of Mount Diablo.

Clayton was nearly called Rhinesville. Joel Clayton and Charles Rhine cofounded the town and each wanted it named after himself. Clayton won, and he and his wife Margaret are buried in Live Oak Cemetery in what is now Concord. The city incorporated in 1964 after a failed attempt in 1960, pushed along by a Concord annexation move in 1963 and by Pleasant Hill's own 1961 incorporation on the other side. The vote on March 3, 1964 carried 251 to 61.

Clayton has 3,990 housing units and 2.1 percent of them predate 1950. 85.8 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 89.2 percent, and the ACS median value is 1,055,200 dollars. ZHVI is about 1,027,000 dollars, up 1.8 percent over the year.

item.content:encoded:
Old Town Danville is the original village centre, and the town around it is younger than the houses.

Danville took four defeats to become a town. Valley wide incorporation went to a vote in 1964, 1967, 1973 and 1976 and failed every time. A home rule campaign started in 1980 and the voters approved it on June 8, 1982.

Eugene O'Neill won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1936 and spent the money building a house above Danville. Tao House is a Monterey Colonial by the architect Frederick Confer, and O'Neill and his wife lived in it from 1937 to 1944. In 1965 three local women, among them Darlene Blair and Lois Sizoo, formed an association to save it, and the place became a National Historic Landmark in 1971, a National Historic Site in 1976, and a National Park Service property in 1980. Getting in is unusual: the site is reached through a private gated road owned by neighbouring residents and visitors cannot drive their own cars to it.

Danville has 16,004 housing units and 1.8 percent of them predate 1950. 77.4 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 85.5 percent. The ACS median value is 1,681,700 dollars and ZHVI is about 1,821,000, up 0.2 percent over the year.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Get the permit history for the parcel.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours, because Old Town mixes retail and residential on adjacent lots. Then ask the town whether the address sits in a historic district or a specific plan area, since that governs what you may change outside.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

  • Crow Canyon. Crow Canyon is the corridor on the southern side of Danville, along the road toward San Ramon.
  • Diablo Road Area. The Diablo Road area runs east out of Danville toward Mount Diablo, and Tao House sits above it.
  • Greenbrook. Greenbrook is a planned residential neighborhood in Danville with its own swim and tennis association.
  • Montair. Montair is a Danville neighborhood that shares its name with the elementary school.
  • Shadow Creek. Shadow Creek is a newer subdivision on the southern edge of Danville.
  • Sycamore. Sycamore is a residential neighborhood on the southern side of Danville.
  • Tassajara. Tassajara is the eastern edge of Danville, out where the town meets ranch ground, and much of the area beyond the line is unincorporated.
  • Westside Danville. Westside Danville is the older residential side of town, west of the main street.

Figure about $16,513 a month to own the typical home in Old Town Danville, $198,157 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

What waiting costs

Danville took four defeats to become a town. Valley wide incorporation went to a vote in 1964, 1967, 1973 and 1976 and failed every time. A home rule campaign started in 1980 and the voters approved it on June 8, 1982.

Eugene O'Neill won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1936 and spent the money building a house above Danville. Tao House is a Monterey Colonial by the architect Frederick Confer, and O'Neill and his wife lived in it from 1937 to 1944. In 1965 three local women, among them Darlene Blair and Lois Sizoo, formed an association to save it, and the place became a National Historic Landmark in 1971, a National Historic Site in 1976, and a National Park Service property in 1980. Getting in is unusual: the site is reached through a private gated road owned by neighbouring residents and visitors cannot drive their own cars to it.

Danville has 16,004 housing units and 1.8 percent of them predate 1950. 77.4 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 85.5 percent. The ACS median value is 1,681,700 dollars and ZHVI is about 1,821,000, up 0.2 percent over the year.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Get the permit history for the parcel.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Westside Danville home is worth $1,821,427. That is up 0.42 percent on the month and up 0.2 percent on the year.

Listing activity in Danville for 2026-09. Active inventory is 135. 80 new listings came on, and 44 went pending. Median days on market is 28.

Median asking price is $1,903,889 at $760 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,821,427, up 0.42 percent month over month, up 0.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $16,513, or $198,157 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Danville I cover, and what each one is:

  • Crow Canyon. Crow Canyon is the corridor on the southern side of Danville, along the road toward San Ramon.
  • Diablo Road Area. The Diablo Road area runs east out of Danville toward Mount Diablo, and Tao House sits above it.
  • Greenbrook. Greenbrook is a planned residential neighborhood in Danville with its own swim and tennis association.
  • Montair. Montair is a Danville neighborhood that shares its name with the elementary school.
  • Old Town Danville. Old Town Danville is the original village centre, and the town around it is younger than the houses.
  • Shadow Creek. Shadow Creek is a newer subdivision on the southern edge of Danville.
  • Sycamore. Sycamore is a residential neighborhood on the southern side of Danville.
  • Tassajara. Tassajara is the eastern edge of Danville, out where the town meets ranch ground, and much of the area beyond the line is unincorporated.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Westside Danville home and the monthly carry lands near $16,513. That is $198,157 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,821,427 here, transfer tax runs about $2,004 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Convention puts about $1,002 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $22,586.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about $10,047, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is $30,434.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

The full report

The full Westside Danville, Danville report carries the month over month tables, the loan and rate detail, the property tax math, the cost of holding, first-time buyer programs, ADU rules and the sources behind every figure. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/danville/westside-danville/.

Danville took four defeats to become a town. Valley wide incorporation went to a vote in 1964, 1967, 1973 and 1976 and failed every time. A home rule campaign started in 1980 and the voters approved it on June 8, 1982.

Eugene O'Neill won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1936 and spent the money building a house above Danville. Tao House is a Monterey Colonial by the architect Frederick Confer, and O'Neill and his wife lived in it from 1937 to 1944. In 1965 three local women, among them Darlene Blair and Lois Sizoo, formed an association to save it, and the place became a National Historic Landmark in 1971, a National Historic Site in 1976, and a National Park Service property in 1980. Getting in is unusual: the site is reached through a private gated road owned by neighbouring residents and visitors cannot drive their own cars to it.

Danville has 16,004 housing units and 1.8 percent of them predate 1950. 77.4 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 85.5 percent. The ACS median value is 1,681,700 dollars and ZHVI is about 1,821,000, up 0.2 percent over the year.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and when each one expires, in writing. A newly built valley subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about the grading and the drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Drive Crow Canyon Road at your real commute hour in both directions. This is the route that carries the valley. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Crow Canyon home is worth $1,821,427. That is up 0.42 percent on the month and up 0.2 percent on the year.

Listing activity in Danville for 2026-09. Active inventory is 135. 80 new listings came on, and 44 went pending. Median days on market is 28.

Median asking price is $1,903,889 at $760 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,821,427, up 0.42 percent month over month, up 0.2 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $16,513, or $198,157 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Danville I cover, and what each one is:

  • Diablo Road Area. The Diablo Road area runs east out of Danville toward Mount Diablo, and Tao House sits above it.
  • Greenbrook. Greenbrook is a planned residential neighborhood in Danville with its own swim and tennis association.
  • Montair. Montair is a Danville neighborhood that shares its name with the elementary school.
  • Old Town Danville. Old Town Danville is the original village centre, and the town around it is younger than the houses.
  • Shadow Creek. Shadow Creek is a newer subdivision on the southern edge of Danville.
  • Sycamore. Sycamore is a residential neighborhood on the southern side of Danville.
  • Tassajara. Tassajara is the eastern edge of Danville, out where the town meets ranch ground, and much of the area beyond the line is unincorporated.
  • Westside Danville. Westside Danville is the older residential side of town, west of the main street.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $16,513 monthly, or $198,157 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. The conforming and FHA ceiling for a one-unit property in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125 in 2026.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

On a home at $1,821,427 here, transfer tax runs about $2,004 at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $1,002 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $22,586.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about $10,047 here. The five year figure is $30,434.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

item.content:encoded:
Downtown San Ramon is newer than the city, and the city is newer than most of its neighbours.

San Ramon incorporated in 1983, and it got there second. Danville lobbied the Local Agency Formation Commission first and succeeded in 1982, and San Ramon followed. The boundary fights before that are worth knowing: the 1967 incorporation proposal covered Alamo, Danville and south San Ramon joined by an 1,800 foot wide cherry stem drawn specifically to leave Bishop Ranch out. In 1978, 585 acres there became the Bishop Ranch business park, and it is the employment base this city was built around.

San Ramon has 30,744 housing units and 0.4 percent of them predate 1950, the newest housing stock of any city in this county. 63.5 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 70.9 percent. The ACS median value is 1,509,500 dollars. ZHVI is about 1,447,000 dollars, down 3.0 percent over the year, and that decline is the only one among the Lamorinda and San Ramon Valley markets.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and when each one expires, in writing. A newly built valley subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about the grading and the drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it, and ask the city whether the address sits inside a specific plan area. In a city built this recently, the plan document tells you what the next decade looks like better than any listing.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

The value index puts a typical Downtown San Ramon home at $1,447,415 on 2026-09-30, up 0.01 percent month over month and down 3.0 percent year over year.

Median asking price is $1,329,250 at $684 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,294, or $159,530 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of San Ramon I cover, and what each one is:

  • Canyon Lakes. Canyon Lakes is a San Ramon community built around a golf course.
  • Country Club. The Country Club neighborhood sits on the eastern side of San Ramon near the golf course.
  • Dougherty Valley. Dougherty Valley is the large planned development on the eastern side of San Ramon, and it is the reason this city's housing stock is the newest in the county.
  • Gale Ranch. Gale Ranch is another of the Dougherty Valley villages, built out over the same period.
  • Henry Ranch. Henry Ranch is a smaller San Ramon subdivision on the higher ground.
  • Twin Creeks. Twin Creeks is one of the older residential neighborhoods in San Ramon, from before incorporation.
  • Westside San Ramon. Westside San Ramon is the older western side of the city, nearer the Bishop Ranch employment base.
  • Windemere. Windemere is one of the Dougherty Valley villages on San Ramon's eastern side.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Downtown San Ramon home and the monthly carry lands near $13,294. That is $159,530 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

As of 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed averages 7.4 percent, up or down from 6.27 percent twelve months before. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $1,592 in transfer tax on a $1,447,415 sale here, at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $796 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,948.

item.content:encoded:
Windemere is one of the Dougherty Valley villages on San Ramon's eastern side.

San Ramon incorporated in 1983, and it got there second. Danville lobbied the Local Agency Formation Commission first and succeeded in 1982, and San Ramon followed. The boundary fights before that are worth knowing: the 1967 incorporation proposal covered Alamo, Danville and south San Ramon joined by an 1,800 foot wide cherry stem drawn specifically to leave Bishop Ranch out. In 1978, 585 acres there became the Bishop Ranch business park, and it is the employment base this city was built around.

San Ramon has 30,744 housing units and 0.4 percent of them predate 1950, the newest housing stock of any city in this county. 63.5 percent are single family detached and owner occupancy runs 70.9 percent. The ACS median value is 1,509,500 dollars. ZHVI is about 1,447,000 dollars, down 3.0 percent over the year, and that decline is the only one among the Lamorinda and San Ramon Valley markets.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and when each one expires, in writing. A newly built valley subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about the grading and the drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Ask which community facilities districts the parcel sits in, what each levies and when each expires, in writing. Then get the association budget and the reserve study and confirm what it maintains. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Windemere is $1,447,415 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.01 percent from the month before and down 3.0 percent over the year.

Listing activity in San Ramon for 2026-09. Active inventory is 135. 58 new listings came on, and 42 went pending. Median days on market is 40.

Median asking price is $1,329,250 at $684 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $1,447,415, up 0.01 percent month over month, down 3.0 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $13,294, or $159,530 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. At the typical value here a minimum-down loan EXCEEDS it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of San Ramon I cover, and what each one is:

  • Canyon Lakes. Canyon Lakes is a San Ramon community built around a golf course.
  • Country Club. The Country Club neighborhood sits on the eastern side of San Ramon near the golf course.
  • Dougherty Valley. Dougherty Valley is the large planned development on the eastern side of San Ramon, and it is the reason this city's housing stock is the newest in the county.
  • Downtown San Ramon. Downtown San Ramon is newer than the city, and the city is newer than most of its neighbours.
  • Gale Ranch. Gale Ranch is another of the Dougherty Valley villages, built out over the same period.
  • Henry Ranch. Henry Ranch is a smaller San Ramon subdivision on the higher ground.
  • Twin Creeks. Twin Creeks is one of the older residential neighborhoods in San Ramon, from before incorporation.
  • Westside San Ramon. Westside San Ramon is the older western side of the city, nearer the Bishop Ranch employment base.

What it costs to own here

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $13,294 monthly, or $159,530 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

The survey average for a 30-year fixed is 7.4 percent at 2026-10-15, compared with 6.27 percent a year back. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Windemere home, $1,447,415, comes to roughly $1,592 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Convention puts about $796 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $17,948.

What waiting costs

Waiting two years at this place's own trailing rate costs about -$99,291, counting the price increase and the payment increase together. Over five years it is -$286,527.

This rests on one observed year carried forward. The two year figure is the defensible one; the five year figure is arithmetic, not a forecast.

The full report

The full Windemere, San Ramon report carries the month over month tables, the loan and rate detail, the property tax math, the cost of holding, first-time buyer programs, ADU rules and the sources behind every figure. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/san-ramon/windemere/.

item.content:encoded:
Rivertown is the original Antioch, down on the San Joaquin River where the landing was.

Antioch started as a river landing. John Marsh, who owned Rancho Los Meganos, built a landing on the San Joaquin in 1848. The Smith twins founded a town just west of it in 1849 and called it Smith's Landing. The place also went by Marsh's Landing and East Antioch before it took the name of the biblical city. The year of that rename is not settled in the sources, so treat any single date for it with suspicion.

Then coal. It was found in 1859 near Horse Haven and the Black Diamond Mine opened in 1860. The boom founded four towns in these hills, Nortonville, Somersville, Stewartville and Black Diamond, and that last one is now the city of Pittsburg. Nortonville was the biggest and the oldest, with a peak population of about 1,000. Sand mining carried on after the coal and ended by the late 1940s, beaten by Belgian glass sand and the closing of the steel foundry. The ground is now Black Diamond Mines Regional Preserve, 6,000 acres under the East Bay Regional Park District.

Antioch has 38,629 housing units and 7.4 percent of them predate 1950. 78.3 percent are single family detached, second only to Brentwood among this county's larger cities. Owner occupancy runs 63.6 percent and the ACS median value is 629,700 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 590,000 dollars, down 0.7 percent over the year.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Rivertown adds two. Pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours, because an original downtown mixes commercial and residential on adjacent lots and a permitted use next door is not always what operates there now. Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

The numbers

  • Monthly cost of owning it: $5,918, or $71,019 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

  • Black Diamond. Black Diamond is named for the coal.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $5,918, $71,019 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

item.content:encoded:
Hillcrest is the Antioch neighborhood around Hillcrest Avenue, on the city's eastern side.

Antioch started as a river landing. John Marsh, who owned Rancho Los Meganos, built a landing on the San Joaquin in 1848. The Smith twins founded a town just west of it in 1849 and called it Smith's Landing. The place also went by Marsh's Landing and East Antioch before it took the name of the biblical city. The year of that rename is not settled in the sources, so treat any single date for it with suspicion.

Then coal. It was found in 1859 near Horse Haven and the Black Diamond Mine opened in 1860. The boom founded four towns in these hills, Nortonville, Somersville, Stewartville and Black Diamond, and that last one is now the city of Pittsburg. Nortonville was the biggest and the oldest, with a peak population of about 1,000. Sand mining carried on after the coal and ended by the late 1940s, beaten by Belgian glass sand and the closing of the steel foundry. The ground is now Black Diamond Mines Regional Preserve, 6,000 acres under the East Bay Regional Park District.

Antioch has 38,629 housing units and 7.4 percent of them predate 1950. 78.3 percent are single family detached, second only to Brentwood among this county's larger cities. Owner occupancy runs 63.6 percent and the ACS median value is 629,700 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 590,000 dollars, down 0.7 percent over the year.

So the buying questions are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

An original kitchen and original aluminium windows are either the discount or the asset. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in.

Then the part specific to this address. BART runs to Antioch now, and the station is the single biggest variable in what an address on this side of the city is worth. Walk to it from the address and time it yourself, and confirm the current service pattern with BART, not a listing, because the line out here does not run the same equipment as the rest of the system. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. It carries the recording date, the original lot dimensions and the street layout as approved, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Typical home value in Hillcrest is $590,401 as of 2026-09-30, up 0.31 percent from the month before and down 0.7 percent over the year.

Listing activity in Antioch for 2026-09. Active inventory is 185. 78 new listings came on, and 90 went pending. Median days on market is 44.

Median asking price is $616,550 at $314 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $590,401, up 0.31 percent month over month, down 0.7 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $5,918, or $71,019 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Antioch I cover, and what each one is:

  • Black Diamond. Black Diamond is named for the coal.
  • Country Hills. Country Hills is a residential subdivision in the Antioch hills.
  • Deer Valley. Deer Valley is on the southern edge of Antioch, out where the city meets open ground.
  • Lone Tree. Lone Tree is the Antioch neighborhood along Lone Tree Way, one of the main east west routes across the city.
  • Mira Vista Hills. Mira Vista Hills is hill ground in Antioch, south of the old river town.
  • Prewett Ranch. Prewett Ranch is a newer Antioch subdivision on the city's southern side.
  • Rivertown. Rivertown is the original Antioch, down on the San Joaquin River where the landing was.
  • Sunset. Sunset is a residential neighborhood in Antioch.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $5,918 a month to own the typical home in Hillcrest, $71,019 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in Contra Costa County tops out at $1,249,125 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $649 in transfer tax on a $590,401 sale here, at 1.10 dollars per thousand. Custom is to split it, so about $325 a side, and who pays is set by the contract.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $7,085.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$9,592 here. The five year figure is -$28,647.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

The full report

The complete Hillcrest, Antioch report runs the tables, the rate and ceiling detail, the tax and holding math, the programs and ADU rules, and dates every source. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/antioch/hillcrest/.

item.content:encoded:
Old Town Pittsburg is the waterfront, and the waterfront is why the city exists.

Pittsburg has had three names. Col. Jonathan D. Stevenson, a New Yorker, bought the Rancho Los Medanos grant in 1849 and founded a town he called New York of the Pacific. It had failed by 1850. Coal out of Nortonville turned the waterfront into a shipping port, and the landing took the name Black Diamond from the mining firm. The town incorporated in 1903 under that name, though some accounts have the post office using Black Diamond as far back as 1868.

Steel made the third name. C.A. Hooper bought the land in 1900 and helped bring in Columbia Steel. The plant opened here in 1910 with one foundry and 60 employees and poured its first heat that November. One source puts the opening at 1906. Columbia Steel became a US Steel subsidiary in 1930 and the mill runs today as USS POSCO. On February 11, 1911 the citizens voted to rename the town Pittsburg, for Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and dropped the h. Camp Stoneman here was a major Army staging area through World War II and Korea.

Pittsburg has 24,482 housing units and 8.3 percent of them predate 1950. 68.2 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 62.3 percent, and the ACS median value is 597,900 dollars. Citywide ZHVI is about 559,000 dollars, down 0.8 percent over the year.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Downtown Oakley was planned before Oakley was a city. The county adopted the Old Town Oakley Specific Plan in 1996, three years before incorporation.

Oakley is the newest city in Contra Costa County. It incorporated on July 1, 1999 and has been reported as the eleventh newest city in the state. The ground was part of Rancho Los Meganos, granted in 1835, and the townsite was settled around 1897 with a post office in 1898. It is a general law city with a council manager government and a five member council elected by district, on the San Joaquin River Delta.

Oakley has 13,944 housing units and 3.0 percent of them predate 1950. 90.6 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 78.8 percent, and the ACS median value is 660,200 dollars. ZHVI is about 654,000 dollars, down 0.5 percent over the year.

So the buying questions are mostly postwar questions.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

An original kitchen and original aluminium windows are either the discount or the asset. The inspection report tells you which.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Read the Old Town Oakley Specific Plan before you write an offer. It is a public document, it is specific about what is intended on these streets, and in a downtown this deliberately planned it tells you more about the next decade than any listing. Then pull the zoning for the parcel and its neighbours.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

Figure about $6,462 a month to own the typical home in Downtown Oakley, $77,542 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

Oakley is the newest city in Contra Costa County. It incorporated on July 1, 1999 and has been reported as the eleventh newest city in the state. The ground was part of Rancho Los Meganos, granted in 1835, and the townsite was settled around 1897 with a post office in 1898. The city planned its downtown before it existed as a city: the work began in the early 1990s while this was still unincorporated, and the county adopted the Old Town Oakley Specific Plan in 1996. It is a general law city with a council manager government and a five member council elected by district, on the San Joaquin River Delta.

Oakley has 13,944 housing units and 3.0 percent of them predate 1950. 90.6 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 78.8 percent, and the ACS median value is 660,200 dollars. ZHVI is about 654,000 dollars, down 0.5 percent over the year.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and the year each one expires, in writing. A newly built East County subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about grading and drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Drive Laurel Road and the Highway 4 corridor at your real commute hour. East County commutes are the single biggest variable in what living here is like. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Laurel is $653,563: up 0.18 percent against last month, down 0.5 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Oakley for 2026-09. Active inventory is 104. 32 new listings came on, and 31 went pending. Median days on market is 44.

Median asking price is $719,350 at $329 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $653,563, up 0.18 percent month over month, down 0.5 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $6,462, or $77,542 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, Contra Costa County: $1,249,125. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.31 percent (Contra Costa County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Oakley I cover, and what each one is:

  • Cypress Grove. Cypress Grove is one of Oakley's newer subdivisions.
  • Downtown Oakley. Downtown Oakley was planned before Oakley was a city.
  • Gardenia. Gardenia is a residential subdivision in Oakley.
  • Magnolia Park. Magnolia Park is a residential subdivision in Oakley.
  • Summer Lake. Summer Lake is a newer Oakley subdivision built around water features.

What it costs to own here

The all-in monthly number for the typical home here is about $6,462, $77,542 over twelve months. It counts the payment, the tax bill, insurance, utilities and a maintenance allowance, and leaves out HOA dues.

The 30-year fixed average is 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent in the same week last year. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in Contra Costa County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Laurel home, $653,563, comes to roughly $719 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Expect it split, near enough $359 apiece, with the contract having the final say.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against El Cerrito at 13.10. Same county, same price, and the spread is $7,843.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$8,280 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$24,786.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

Westside Alamo is the hill side of this unincorporated community, up toward the Las Trampas ridge.

The ACS reports a median owner occupied value of 2,000,001 dollars here, and that is the survey's ceiling, not a measurement. The actual median sits above the highest figure the survey will print.

Ask the inspector about soils and drainage on the parcel and about where water leaves it in a wet month. Ask about the condition and the ownership of every retaining structure, because a shared retaining wall on a slope is the most expensive thing that can go wrong.

Get a written fire insurance quote on the exact address with the risk rating explained, and ask what the insurer wants cleared to write it. In this part of the county that quote decides deals.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

And it is set by the city, not the county. Antioch charges 1.10 per thousand against Richmond at 13.50. Same county, same price, and the spread is $31,365.

Blackhawk is a gated community and it is not a city.

Blackhawk is unincorporated Contra Costa County territory on the eastern side of the San Ramon Valley, below Mount Diablo. The valley's towns incorporated around it, Danville in 1982 after voters approved it on June 8 of that year, and San Ramon in 1983, following four failed valley wide attempts in 1964, 1967, 1973 and 1976. Blackhawk remained county ground and it is governed as a private community inside it.

The man who built it left a museum behind. Kenneth Behring developed Blackhawk, and a partnership he began with Don Williams in 1982 opened the Blackhawk Automotive Museum in August 1988, called the Behring Auto Museum in some accounts. It started as a home for his car collection and now runs four more galleries alongside it: The Spirit of the Old West, Art of Africa, Into China and World of Nature. It is a subsidiary of the non profit Behring Global Educational Foundation and an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution. It sits inside Blackhawk Plaza and is not affiliated with the shopping centre. Behring also owned the Seattle Seahawks and founded the Wheelchair Foundation. He died in 2019 at 91.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and the year each one expires, in writing. A newly built East County subdivision can carry a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Get the flood zone determination for the parcel with a written insurance quote, and ask the inspector about settlement and about the condition and ownership of any bulkhead, levee or revetment the property sits behind. On the water that is the most expensive thing that can go wrong and it is frequently shared. Ask who owns and who maintains the channel and the dock, get the dock permit and its condition in writing, and ask whether dredging is an association obligation and when it was last done. Kensington is unincorporated Contra Costa County territory on the hill above Berkeley and El Cerrito, and it has never incorporated. Kensington stayed county ground.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history for the parcel.

In a place where nearly 60 percent of the housing is pre war and nearly all of it sits on a slope, those two lists are the whole purchase.

In an unincorporated place the service districts are the government, and Kensington's are unusually well documented. The Kensington Police Protection and Community Services District was formed in 1946, first as the Kensington Police Protection District, and reorganised under the community services district law in 1953. Accounts of its renaming differ, a community timeline giving 1993 and the county's LAFCO giving 1995. Fire ran separately for most of that time: the Kensington Fire Protection District was formed in 1937 and in 1995 it contracted with the City of El Cerrito for fire and emergency service. Effective October 1, 2025 the fire district consolidated into the community services district.

So ask who answers a call at this address and under which district, and ask what each district levies on the parcel. In a place with no city, those are the questions a city would otherwise answer for you.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

On July 17, 1944 at 10:08 at night an explosion there killed 320 men, the worst stateside disaster of World War II. The trial that followed was the largest naval mutiny case in United States history and it led to the desegregation of the Navy. item.content:encoded:
Spanos Park is on the northern edge of Stockton.

Stockton exists because a man gave up on gold. Captain Charles Maria Weber, who came from Germany, acquired Rancho Campo de los Franceses and founded the town in 1849. He tried mining first and worked out that selling supplies to the people going to the mines paid better. The site sat at the head of navigation on the San Joaquin River, so the goods came by water and the miners came to him. He laid the place out as Tuleburg and then settled on Stockton, for Commodore Robert F. Stockton. The city incorporated on July 23, 1850 and took its charter from the state in 1851.

The other thing every buyer here should know is the bankruptcy, because it is finished and the facts are public. Stockton filed Chapter 9 on July 28, 2012 against more than 2 billion dollars in labour agreements and long term debt, the largest bankrupt city in the country until Detroit filed the next year. A judge found it eligible on April 1, 2013. Chief Bankruptcy Judge Christopher Klein confirmed the plan of adjustment on October 30, 2014 and signed the confirmation order on February 4, 2015, and the city exited effective February 25, 2015. Every major creditor settled except Franklin Templeton Investments. The payment schedule under that plan runs to 2053.

Stockton has 105,162 housing units and 13.8 percent of them predate 1950. 66.8 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 53.9 percent, and the ACS median value is 440,900 dollars. ZHVI is about 422,000 dollars, down 1.7 percent over the year, the lowest level of any city in the three counties covered here.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and the year each one expires, in writing. A newly built Central Valley subdivision frequently carries a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about grading and drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the tract map for the subdivision from the county recorder. The recording date, the original lot dimensions and the approved street layout are all on it, and that record beats anything a listing will tell you about when and how this neighborhood was built.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

Measured to 2026-09-30, typical value in Spanos Park is $422,451: up 0.10 percent against last month, down 1.7 percent against last year.

Listing activity in Stockton for 2026-09. Active inventory is 557. 218 new listings came on, and 251 went pending. Median days on market is 59.

Median asking price is $423,750 at $279 per square foot.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $422,451, up 0.10 percent month over month, down 1.7 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $4,459, or $53,505 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, San Joaquin County: $832,750. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.27 percent (Stockton effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Stockton I cover, and what each one is:

  • Airport District. The Airport District is south of downtown Stockton, around the airport.
  • August. August is an older neighborhood on Stockton's east side.
  • Banner Island. Banner Island is on the downtown Stockton waterfront.
  • Bear Creek. Bear Creek runs through north Stockton and the neighborhood takes its name.
  • Boggs Tract. Boggs Tract sits against Stockton's working industrial waterfront.
  • Brookside Estates. Brookside Estates is part of the Brookside development in north Stockton.
  • Brookside. Brookside is a north Stockton community built around waterways and a golf course.
  • Cabral. Cabral is a Stockton residential neighborhood.

What it costs to own here

Figure about $4,459 a month to own the typical home in Spanos Park, $53,505 a year. Loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance are in that figure. HOA dues are not, and they vary too much to average.

On 2026-10-15 the 30-year fixed average was 7.4 percent, where the year-ago figure was 6.27 percent. For 2026, one-unit financing in San Joaquin County tops out at $832,750 on both the conforming and the FHA side.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Figure $465 in transfer tax on a $422,451 sale here, at 1.10 dollars per thousand. It is normally split down the middle, about $232 on each party. The contract governs, not the custom.

What waiting costs

On the same trailing rate, two years of waiting adds up to roughly -$16,396 in price and payment combined, and five years to -$48,252.

One year of data, extended. That is worth saying plainly, because compounding it out to five years makes the total look more certain than it is.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

  • Brookside Estates. Brookside Estates is part of the Brookside development in north Stockton.
  • Brookside. Brookside is a north Stockton community built around waterways and a golf course.
  • Cabral. Cabral is a Stockton residential neighborhood.

item.content:encoded:
Garden Acres is on Stockton's eastern side and part of this area is unincorporated county ground.

Stockton filed Chapter 9 on July 28, 2012 against more than 2 billion dollars in labour agreements and long term debt, the largest bankrupt city in the country until Detroit filed the next year. A judge found it eligible on April 1, 2013. Chief Bankruptcy Judge Christopher Klein confirmed the plan of adjustment on October 30, 2014 and signed the confirmation order on February 4, 2015, and the city exited effective February 25, 2015. Every major creditor settled except Franklin Templeton Investments. The payment schedule under that plan runs to 2053.

Stockton has 105,162 housing units and 13.8 percent of them predate 1950. 66.8 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 53.9 percent, and the ACS median value is 440,900 dollars. ZHVI is about 422,000 dollars, down 1.7 percent over the year, the lowest level of any city in the three counties covered here.

Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

Ask whether the parcel is on sewer or on septic, and if septic, get the most recent inspection and the pumping record. Ask whether water comes from a district or a well, and if a well, get the yield and the water quality tests in writing. On valley agricultural ground, also ask what is farmed on the adjoining parcels and when it is sprayed.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

  • Boggs Tract. Boggs Tract sits against Stockton's working industrial waterfront.
  • Brookside Estates. Brookside Estates is part of the Brookside development in north Stockton.
  • Brookside. Brookside is a north Stockton community built around waterways and a golf course.
  • Cabral. Cabral is a Stockton residential neighborhood.

Carry on the typical home here is roughly $4,459 monthly, or $53,505 annually. That covers the loan payment, property tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance at a stated budget. HOA dues are excluded, because they differ building to building.

That rate is one observed year extrapolated forward, not a forecast, and compounding a single strong year out to five produces a large number by construction. Weight the two year figure more heavily.

item.content:encoded:
Downtown Lodi is where the arch stands, and 15.9 percent of this city's housing predates 1950. A good share of it is here.

Lodi started as a railroad stop called Mokelumne Station, when the Central Pacific put a station here in 1869. The renaming is a genuine muddle. A city page says the Legislature changed the name in 1874, to stop the confusion with Mokelumne City and Mokelumne Hill. Britannica gives 1873 and suggests a racehorse of the day. A city records finding aid says the residents did it themselves in 1878. Another account credits Assembly Bill 639 and points at Lodi, Italy. Residents voted on incorporation in 1906 and the county Board of Supervisors declared Lodi incorporated on December 6 of that year.

The arch is the landmark. E. B. Brown built it in 1907 for the first Lodi Tokay Carnival, an event that exists today as the Lodi Grape Festival, and a city page calls it the oldest standing welcome arch in the United States. It was restored in 1956 after it had deteriorated into a hazard. The carnival was built around the Flame Tokay, a grape developed here, and the whole point of it in 1907 was to advertise that grape.

Lodi has 24,806 housing units and 15.9 percent of them predate 1950, the highest pre war share of any city in San Joaquin County. 64.9 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 56.8 percent, and the ACS median value is 492,500 dollars. ZHVI is about 509,000 dollars, down 1.4 percent over the year.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history for the parcel.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it, because this part of the city puts commercial or industrial use on lots next to housing and a permitted use next door is not always what operates there now. Then ask the city whether the address sits inside a downtown specific plan or historic area. And a practical warning on your own research: published hours for downtown businesses conflict across the visitor bureau, the chamber and the local paper, so confirm days and verify hours directly.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

$508,738 is the typical Downtown Lodi home as of 2026-09-30. Month over month that is up 0.06 percent, and over the year down 1.4 percent.

item.content:encoded:
Downtown Tracy grew around the railroad junction of 1878.

Tracy is a railroad town and the date is exact. It was founded on September 8, 1878 and named for Lathrop J. Tracy, a grain merchant and railroad director from Mansfield, Ohio, who as far as the record shows never lived here. The town came out of a junction: Southern Pacific built its line around Suisun Bay in September 1878 and made the connection three miles east of Ellis, with one account calling it a Central Pacific junction. The railroad shut the Ellis coaling station and moved its employees and their families to Lathrop and to the new Tracy station. Southern Pacific moved its operational headquarters from Lathrop to Tracy in 1894. Tracy became a city in 1910.

Tracy has 30,228 housing units and 7.1 percent of them predate 1950. 81.0 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 65.0 percent, and the ACS median value is 699,000 dollars. ZHVI is about 668,000 dollars, down 4.1 percent over the year. That is the steepest twelve month decline of any city in San Joaquin County, and among the steepest in the three counties covered here. A buyer should know it going in.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history for the parcel.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it, because this part of the city puts commercial or industrial use on lots next to housing and a permitted use next door is not always what operates there now. Tracy has 30,228 housing units and 7.1 percent of them predate 1950. 81.0 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 65.0 percent, and the ACS median value is 699,000 dollars. ZHVI is about 668,000 dollars, down 4.1 percent over the year. That is the steepest twelve month decline of any city in San Joaquin County, and among the steepest in the three counties covered here. Pull the year built and the permit history for the parcel. On a tract house of this era, ask about the electrical panel and its capacity, the supply lines, the sewer lateral, the roof, and whether the foundation has ever been bolted.

item.content:encoded:
Questa is one of the planned villages of Mountain House.

Mountain House is the newest city in California. It became the state's 483rd city on July 1, 2024, after voters approved Measures D and E on March 5 of that year, and before that it was a community services district. The place was planned long before it was a city: San Joaquin County adopted the Mountain House Master Plan as a General Plan amendment in 1993, the Board of Supervisors approved the planned community in 1994, and construction started in 2001. The Yokuts were the original inhabitants of this ground. In 1849 Thomas Goodall put up a tent of blue denim cloth here as a midway stop for miners heading from San Francisco over Altamont Pass to the Sierra foothills.

Mountain House has 7,349 housing units and 3.1 percent of them predate 1950. 83.5 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 69.9 percent, and the ACS median value is 946,900 dollars, the highest of any place in San Joaquin County. Zillow publishes no value series under the Mountain House name, so the figure on this page is the one for ZIP 95391. That ZIP covers the town, Zillow labels it Tracy, and it reads about 848,000 dollars, down 8.0 percent over the year. It is the best available measure and it is not a Mountain House city index, so read it as the ZIP figure it is and work from closed comparable sales on the specific streets.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Mountain House is laid out as a set of named villages, each planned as a unit, so pull the village's own plan and tract map from the county and read what was approved. And one thing specific to a city this new. A municipality incorporated in 2024 is still building out its own services, its own revenue base and its own general plan, so ask the city directly what it now provides and what the county or a district still provides, and ask what the community services district's obligations became on incorporation. Mountain House is the newest city in California. It became the state's 483rd city on July 1, 2024, after voters approved Measures D and E on March 5 of that year, and before that it was a community services district. The place was planned long before it was a city: San Joaquin County adopted the Mountain House Master Plan as a General Plan amendment in 1993, the Board of Supervisors approved the planned community in 1994, and construction started in 2001. The Yokuts were the original inhabitants of this ground. In 1849 Thomas Goodall put up a tent of blue denim cloth here as a midway stop for miners heading from San Francisco over Altamont Pass to the Sierra foothills.

Mountain House has 7,349 housing units and 3.1 percent of them predate 1950. 83.5 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 69.9 percent, and the ACS median value is 946,900 dollars, the highest of any place in San Joaquin County. Zillow publishes no value series under the Mountain House name, so the figure on this page is the one for ZIP 95391. That ZIP covers the town, Zillow labels it Tracy, and it reads about 848,000 dollars, down 8.0 percent over the year. It is the best available measure and it is not a Mountain House city index, so read it as the ZIP figure it is and work from closed comparable sales on the specific streets.

So the buying questions here are newer-construction questions.

Get the homeowners association budget and the reserve study, not the dues figure, and ask exactly what the association maintains and what it does not.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate, and ask which assessment districts the parcel sits in and the year each one expires, in writing. A newly built Central Valley subdivision frequently carries a community facilities district on top of the base rate, and that line runs for decades and does not come off with the mortgage.

Then ask the inspector about grading and drainage, because a young subdivision on engineered fill shows its settlement in the first fifteen years.

Then the part specific to this address. Mountain House is laid out as a set of named villages, each planned as a unit, so pull the village's own plan and tract map from the county and read what was approved. And one thing specific to a city this new. A municipality incorporated in 2024 is still building out its own services, its own revenue base and its own general plan, so ask the city directly what it now provides and what the county or a district still provides, and ask what the community services district's obligations became on incorporation. Those answers determine your tax bill and your services and they are changing.

Then drive your commute at the hour you would really drive it, and walk the block after dinner.

What the market is doing right now

As of 2026-09-30 the typical Bethany home is worth $848,137. That is down 1.12 percent on the month and down 8.0 percent on the year.

Realtor.com does not publish monthly listing metrics for Mountain House, so there is no inventory, days on market or asking price figure to report here. The value series above is measured separately and is unaffected.

The numbers

  • Typical home value: $848,137, down 1.12 percent month over month, down 8.0 percent over the year.
  • Monthly cost of owning it: $8,080, or $96,959 a year, HOA not included.
  • 30-year fixed: 7.4 percent as of 2026-10-15, against 6.27 percent a year earlier.
  • 2026 one-unit loan limit, San Joaquin County: $832,750. A minimum-down loan at the typical value sits inside it.
  • Effective property tax rate used: 1.23 percent (San Joaquin County effective rate).

Inside it

For context, the other parts of Mountain House I cover, and what each one is:

  • Altamont. Altamont is a Mountain House village, and the pass it is named for carried the 1849 miners.
  • College Park. College Park is one of the Mountain House villages.
  • Cordes. Cordes is a Mountain House village.
  • Hansen. Hansen is a Mountain House village.
  • Questa. Questa is one of the planned villages of Mountain House.
  • Wicklund. Wicklund is one of the planned villages in Mountain House.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Bethany home and the monthly carry lands near $8,080. That is $96,959 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

Rates sit at 7.4 percent on the 30-year fixed as of 2026-10-15. A year earlier the same survey read 6.27 percent. The 2026 one-unit loan limit in San Joaquin County is $832,750, and that figure is both the conforming ceiling and the FHA ceiling.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Bethany home, $848,137, comes to roughly $933 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Convention puts about $466 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

What waiting costs

The two year cost of waiting, price plus payment, comes to about -$152,069 here. The five year figure is -$407,186.

Treat it as a scenario, not a prediction. The appreciation input is one year of observed change carried forward, and five years of compounding on one year of data flatters the result.

The full report

Everything behind these numbers lives in the full Bethany, Mountain House report: the tables, the rate and loan detail, the tax math, holding costs, buyer programs, ADU rules and a dated source for each figure. It is rebuilt every month when the new data publishes. Read it at https://myrealtoraye.github.io/neighborhood-reports/mountain-house/bethany/.

item.title: Downtown Manteca, Manteca: the October 2026 read
item.description: What the Downtown Manteca, Manteca housing market is doing in October 2026. Typical value $572,552, down 0.11 percent month over month, plus the transfer tax bracket that costs real money and what waiting actually costs.
item.content:encoded:
Downtown Manteca grew around the 1873 railroad stop that got its name misprinted.

Manteca is named after a typographical error. Joshua Cowell arrived in 1861 and the place carried his name, but when the Central Pacific came through in 1873 a new one was needed, because a Cowell's Station already existed to the south near Tracy. They settled on Monteca and the first railroad tickets came back printed Manteca. The Manteca Bulletin treats the ticket misprint as the account with the most credence; a weaker telling puts the error in a newspaper. The town incorporated in 1918, with May 28 given as the date, and Cowell became its first mayor.

The rail line that named this town shaped the whole southern end of the county. The Central Pacific came through here in 1873 and the farm towns along it, Ripon and Escalon among them, sit where they do because of it. Ripon was called Stanislaus Station before it was Ripon. Tracy, twenty miles west, was founded on September 8, 1878 at a junction Southern Pacific built around Suisun Bay, and it took the headquarters away from Lathrop in 1894.

Downtown Ripon is a small valley town centre.

Ripon was called Stanislaus Station first. The town's first settler took a claim near the Stanislaus River, the community grew around the station, and the name changed later. The city incorporated in 1945, with the Chamber of Commerce as the sponsor of the effort, and both the city's own history and the standard reference give that year; a tourism site claiming March 1913 is contradicted by the official record. Almonds are a documented part of the local economy and the orchards are still the landscape here.

The railroad shaped this part of the valley the way it shaped the rest. The Central Pacific came through neighbouring Manteca in 1873, and that line is why the towns along it sit where they do. Manteca got its name from a misprint on the first tickets printed after that line arrived.

Ripon has 5,742 housing units and 4.1 percent of them predate 1950. 79.5 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 65.8 percent, and the ACS median value is 704,800 dollars. ZHVI is about 674,000 dollars, up 0.3 percent over the year, one of only a handful of places in this county that rose.

So the first questions here are the old housing questions.

Pull the year built. On pre war stock, ask about foundation bolting, knob and tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, and the condition of the original windows and siding. Confirm the legal unit count with the city, not the listing, and get the permit history for the parcel.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it, because this part of the city puts commercial or industrial use on lots next to housing and a permitted use next door is not always what operates there now.

What it costs to own here

Put the minimum down on the typical Downtown Ripon home and the monthly carry lands near $6,512. That is $78,146 across a year, counting loan, tax, insurance, utilities and maintenance. HOA dues are not in it, since no two are alike.

The transfer tax line that costs real money

Transfer tax on the typical Downtown Ripon home, $673,757, comes to roughly $741 at a rate of 1.10 per thousand. Convention puts about $371 on each side of the table. That is custom, and it is negotiable.

What waiting costs

Hold off two years and the combined price and payment cost is near $3,945. At five years it reaches $11,952.

Downtown Escalon is the centre of a small orchard-country city.

Escalon is a small city in the orchard country at the southern end of San Joaquin County, on the rail line that shaped this part of the valley. The Central Pacific came through neighbouring Manteca in 1873, and Manteca got its name from a misprint on the first tickets printed after that line arrived. Escalon itself incorporated on March 12, 1957 by the standard reference, though that date rests on a single source; a club history from around 1917 describes the town as not then incorporated. That is at least consistent with a later date.

Escalon has 2,905 housing units and 7.1 percent of them predate 1950. 87.7 percent are single family detached, owner occupancy runs 72.4 percent, and the ACS median value is 471,200 dollars. ZHVI is about 591,000 dollars, up 1.1 percent over the year.

Ask whether the building is nonconforming, because that limits what you can rebuild after a loss and it affects financing and insurance.

Get the tax bill for the address, not the listing estimate.

Then the part specific to this address. Pull the zoning for the parcel and everything touching it, because this part of the city puts commercial or industrial use on lots next to housing and a permitted use next door is not always what operates there now. Ask whether the parcel is on sewer or on septic, and if septic, get the most recent inspection and the pumping record.
